title: Scaffold pnpm monorepo: apps/web + packages/*
description:
Create the pnpm-workspace monorepo skeleton for Agent Battle, exactly as specified in the plan section 19 (Implementation - monorepo layout).

WHY FIRST: The plan locks a specific target layout because several architectural guarantees are enforced by the folder boundaries themselves (section 19 dependency rule, section 33 extension kinds). If the scaffold deviates, the guarantees 'features never import each other' and 'adding a feature never edits core/cli/mcp' become unenforceable conventions instead of structural facts.

CREATE per section 19:
- package.json (pnpm workspaces), pnpm-workspace.yaml, turbo.json (optional)
- .env.example with BETTER_AUTH_SECRET, BETTER_AUTH_URL, GITHUB_CLIENT_ID, GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET, DATABASE_URL
- apps/web/ (Next.js 14 App Router: pages, api routes, components, lib)
- packages/core/ (primitives ONLY, no game words)
- packages/protocol/ (versioned AgentEvent union, tool-map, version.ts)
- packages/adapters/{claude,codex,opencode,cursor,pi,gemini,_template}/
- packages/features/{agent,progression,reputation,quest,bounty,battle,guild,social,inventory,animation}/
- packages/game-client/ (PixiJS v8 world)
- packages/mcp-server/ (thin, 5 stable primitives only)
- packages/cli/ (P0 per sections 31/36)
- drizzle/ (schema + migrations), scripts/

DEPENDENCY DIRECTION (enforced separately): presentation -> features -> core <- infrastructure. Features NEVER import each other (only core + protocol). Adapters import core + protocol only.

CONSIDERATIONS: Docker lives in the infrastructure layer only (section 37) - features must never import Docker/Compose/Postgres-container concepts, only repository/capability interfaces (section 33). Folders may start near-empty; this bead establishes structural boundaries, not contents.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: pnpm install succeeds; pnpm -r build runs (each package may be a stub); folder graph matches section 19 exactly; no package imports outside its allowed direction.

TESTS: a scaffolding test that walks packages/* and asserts each has package.json with the correct @battle-agents/* name and no cross-boundary imports.
close_reason: Scaffold verified: 24 packages, pnpm build and pnpm -r typecheck green, architecture and removal-test gates pass

title: Lock MIT license + THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES + license CI check
description:
Establish license hygiene for the whole repo, per plan section 35 (License lock: MIT) and section 28.3 (Attribution hygiene, CI-enforced).

WHY P0 AND NOT POLISH: The project vendors/ports substantial third-party code. Section 28.1 lists 12 direct-copy items drawn from 8 repos under 4 different licenses. Getting attribution right AFTER copying is far harder and riskier than establishing the mechanism first. Section 35 also records that the plan previously contradicted itself on MIT vs Apache-2.0, so the lock must be explicit or the ambiguity will creep back.

VERIFIED LICENSE FACTS (from .tmp checkouts, plan section 28):
- MIT: agent-dashboard, agent-quest, arcane-agents, moltbook, paperclip, pixel-agents, tmux-agents, age-of-agents, cross-agent-teams-mcp, agent-move, agent-world-codemoo
- Apache-2.0: agent-world-smallville
- MPL-2.0: agentworld-openagents (Kaetram fork - FILE-LEVEL copyleft)
- CC0: agent-quest tiny-swords-cc0 asset pack

RULES per section 28:
- MIT / Apache-2.0 / CC0: may copy with attribution (keep the copyright header, add a THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES entry).
- MPL-2.0: NEVER paste Kaetram files into our tree; the copyleft attaches to those files. Learn the pattern only, rewrite clean in TypeScript.
- No-license-confirmed (learn-spine until verified): hands off, copy NOTHING.

CREATE:
- LICENSE (MIT; the file already exists - verify its content matches the section 35 decision)
- THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md at repo root: every copied/ported file listed with source repo + commit SHA + license
- scripts/check-licenses.sh: fails CI if any file under packages/ or apps/ matches an MPL-2.0 header or a Kaetram import path. Allowlist: MIT / Apache-2.0 / CC0 only.
- Game art keeps its OWN license file beside each pack (public/assets/<pack>/LICENSE.txt). Asset licenses are tracked separately from the MIT code license (sections 14, 17.7).

CONSIDERATIONS: Section 28.3 explicitly separates the MIT code license from per-pack asset licenses. Do not collapse these. Section 35: any future Apache-2.0 mention elsewhere in docs is stale unless a new explicit decision reverses the lock.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: scripts/check-licenses.sh runs in CI and passes on a clean tree; it FAILS on a deliberately planted MPL-2.0 header (proving the guard works); THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md exists and names the source repos.

TESTS: unit test for the license scanner (pattern match, allowlist, exit code) plus a negative test that plants a forbidden header and asserts a non-zero exit.
close_reason: Verified: LICENSE is MIT, THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md names 6 source repos, check-licenses.sh has a self-test that plants forbidden headers and asserts denial, and the stage runs in CI via test:m0. Gate passes.

title: Enforce dependency direction (features never cross-import)
description:
Machine-enforce the plan section 19 dependency rule and the section 33 extension-kind boundary so the architecture cannot silently rot.

THE RULE (section 19): presentation -> features -> core <- infrastructure. Features NEVER import each other (only core + protocol). Adapters import core + protocol only.

WHY: Section 12.1 declares the God-Engine antipattern (a GameEngine accumulating if(hasBounty)/if(hasGuild) branches into 4000 LOC of unremovable features) to be BANNED. The stated architectural principle number 1 is the REMOVAL TEST: rm -rf features/guild must still compile and run. That property only holds if the boundary is enforced mechanically rather than by discipline.

IMPLEMENT dependency-cruiser config (or eslint no-restricted-imports) encoding:
- features/* may import core/*, protocol/*, and their own files. NOT other features/*.
- core/* may import nothing from features/, adapters/, interfaces/, infrastructure/.
- adapters/* may import core/*, protocol/* only. NEVER game code (section 23: 'No adapter imports game code - ever').
- interfaces/{cli,mcp,api,websocket}/* consume features through the capability registry, never by importing feature implementations (section 36).
- infrastructure/* may import core/* only; features never import Docker/Compose/Postgres-container concepts (section 37).

REVIEW CHECKLIST ENFORCEMENT (sections 33, 36): any PR that forces edits to core/, cli/, or mcp/ implementations in order to add a feature is an ARCHITECTURE FAILURE. Allowed: composition-root/manifest one-liners. Any PR adding interfaces/cli/* or interfaces/mcp/* implementation code FOR A SPECIFIC GAME FEATURE (instead of registry entries) also fails review.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: adding a deliberately illegal import makes lint/build fail with a message naming the violated rule; the dependency graph report shows clean layering.

TESTS: a unit test running the rule engine over a fixture tree containing each violation type, asserting each is caught.

CONSIDERATIONS: a lint rule that fires on legitimate code is worse than no rule, because teams disable it. Expect false positives during the initial port of the age-of-agents client and the learn-spine-derived animation core, both of which are structured differently from our conventions. Add narrow, documented exceptions rather than weakening the rule. Also worth encoding in CI rather than review: architecture failures are exactly the kind of thing a reviewer waves through under deadline pressure, and this is the mechanism that makes 'adding a feature never edits core' a fact rather than an aspiration.
close_reason: Verified: architecture-rules.cjs exports the engine, a test exercises every declared rule against a fixture and asserts nothing else fires, violations name the rule, and the real tree reports 0 violations. Stage runs in CI via test:m0.

title: Removal test: every feature removable without breaking the build
description:
Turn the REMOVAL TEST into an executable CI gate, per plan section 12.2 and section 20.

WHAT IT IS: Section 12.2 states 'Removal test is architectural principle #1: rm -rf features/guild must still compile/run.' This bead makes that principle an automated check so the pluggability property cannot silently regress as features are added.

MECHANISM (section 20): scripts/removal-test.sh - for each packages/features/*, temporarily move it away, then run 'tsc --noEmit && vitest run'. The tree must stay GREEN except for capability-degraded warnings. This is also the mechanism by which the Battle feature proves its requires: ['reputation.read'] degradation (section 24).

WHY IT MATTERS: The entire extension architecture (sections 12, 33) is justified by 'add feature without touching others'. If removal breaks the build, the architecture has quietly become a God Engine and section 29.2's 'thin core, rich edges' claim is false. Catching that in CI rather than at M6 is the entire value of this bead.

CONSIDERATIONS: the script MUST restore the moved directory even on failure (trap/finally), or a crashed run leaves the tree broken. It must be reasonably fast so it runs in CI and not just locally. Capability-degraded warnings (a feature whose requires[] become unsatisfied after removal) are EXPECTED and must not fail the run; only type errors and test failures do.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: 'pnpm removal-test' passes with all features present; passes with any single feature removed; fails when a feature illegally imports a sibling feature (cross-check with the dependency-rules bead).

TESTS: the script is itself the test. Add a fixture feature that illegally imports a sibling and assert the removal-test run fails.
close_reason: Script checks all 10 removable features + extensions[] stripping; self-test proves the strip is sound and was mutation-verified against the exact bug it guards. Gate runs in CI via test:m0.

title: CONTRACT 2: Agent Identity - agents + credentials + ownership
description:
Implement and FREEZE Contract 2: Agent Identity, per plan section 29.1 and section 38.

THE INVARIANT (section 29.1 item 2, and section 38): the agents row plus agent_credentials (hash, scopes, expiry) plus ownership via agents.user_id. 'GitHub User ID is NOT Agent ID, permanently.' The invariant sessions.agent_id -> agents.id is load-bearing.

SCHEMA per plan section 21:
- users: id, githubId (unique), login, avatarUrl, createdAt
- installations: id, userId -> users, installationKey (unique), label, lastSeenAt, createdAt
- agents: id, userId -> users, name, harness, level, xp, reputation, build, status, lastSeenAt, createdAt
- agent_credentials: id, installationId -> installations, tokenHash, scopes, expiresAt, revokedAt, createdAt

HARD SEPARATIONS (section 38, enforce in code review):
- Better Auth owns User/Auth/human-Session ONLY. The game domain stays in extensions.
- The GitHub OAuth token is NEVER agent identity. The chain is: User (human) -> Agent (persistent character: XP/level/rep + credential + sessions) -> Session (one run) -> Credential (the token the agent calls back with). Example: User#42 -> Agent 'CodeKnight' (1250 XP, Lv 7, Rep 83) -> Sessions #a1/#b7.
- Agent credential issuance/rotation endpoints live under the Agent extension, NOT inside Better Auth config.

WHY AGENT IS PERSISTENT AND SESSION IS EPHEMERAL (plan section 3.1-3.2): AGENT is never deleted when a terminal closes. It holds XP/level/skills/build/reputation/inventory/achievements/battle+quest history. This is the plan's 'most important design' (section 3 heading) and the basis of the whole social/network-effect story (section 2.4).

IDENTITY RESOLUTION (section 3.2): do NOT key on process name alone - three concurrent Claudes must stay distinguishable. Resolution uses agent_id + installation_id + project_id + session_id. installation_id is generated once at install (~/.agent-battle/identity.json {installationId}). Multi-machine: GitHub User -> Agent -> Installations (PC/Laptop/Server/WSL/Docker) -> Sessions.

TOKEN MODEL (section 3.4): a token authenticates a user/installation and NEVER equals a session. Close -> #003 CLOSED; reopen -> #004 CREATED under the same User/Claude. NEVER put raw tokens in MCP URLs (?token= leaks into logs and history) - use MCP OAuth -> short-lived access tokens. Web GitHub login and MCP agent authorization are related but SEPARATE credentials.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: schema exists with the FK chain users -> agents -> sessions and the invariant sessions.agent_id -> agents.id enforced at the DB level; credentials store a HASH (never the raw token); ownership is queryable.

TESTS: migration test; a test that agent_credentials stores only a hash (assert the raw token is absent from the row); a test that a user's agent cannot be read by another user (authorization at the repository boundary).

CONSIDERATIONS: the separation of four ID classes - permanent identity, credential, session, event - is easy to blur and expensive to undo. Agent is the character and persists forever; credential is a revocable secret; session is an ephemeral run; event is a log entry. Keeping them distinct is what makes 'close the terminal, reopen tomorrow, same character' possible. The multi-installation case (PC, laptop, server, WSL, Docker) is not hypothetical - get the schema right for it now rather than retrofitting a second installation concept later.
close_reason: CONTRACT 2. Schema half pre-existing (users -> installations/agents -> agent_credentials/sessions, tokenHash only, sessions.agent_id -> agents.id). Added the feature: four id classes branded so they cannot be passed for one another, ownership a required parameter on every repository method, codes as the cross-layer error contract (instanceof cannot work across the layering boundary). 12 unit tests + 8 integration tests against live Postgres proving a user's agent cannot be read by another user. Found and fixed: agents_user_id_name_unique was declared index not uniqueIndex, so the DB never enforced one name per owner (migration 0001). drizzle/ moved to packages/db/ so a store can be depended on. Removal test proves the feature is independently removable.

title: CONTRACT 3: Session lifecycle + HELLO resume-vs-new handshake
description:
Implement and FREEZE Contract 3: Session, per plan section 29.1 item 3, section 3.2, and section 22.

THE INVARIANT: sessions.agent_id -> agents.id, NEVER sessions.user_id as agent identity (section 29.1).

SCHEMA (section 21): sessions: id, agentId -> agents, installationId -> installations, projectId -> projects (nullable), harnessSessionRef, status (default 'active'), startedAt, endedAt, lastHeartbeatAt.

SESSION LIFECYCLE (section 3.2):
- Terminal close: Session -> CLOSED; Agent ACTIVE -> OFFLINE; stats persist (Level/XP/Battles/Tests/Last-seen).
- Reopen must NOT create 'Claude #2'. Identity resolution maps a new process to the SAME Agent, producing old Session#182 + new Session#205.
- State machine: ACTIVE -> COMPLETED / STOPPED(ABANDONED) / CRASHED / TIMEOUT(DISCONNECTED).
- Battle states (separate machine): RUNNING / PAUSED / COMPLETED / ABANDONED / EXPIRED.
- Disconnect during a battle -> grace period -> reconnect? resume : abandoned.
- MVP may skip the Run layer (Agent -> Run -> Session) and keep Agent -> Session only.

HELLO HANDSHAKE (section 22): POST /api/sessions receives {installationKey, agentName, harness, projectRepoUrl?}. It must find-or-create installation/agent/project, then look for a status=disconnected session with the same agent+installation+project within a grace window (default 15 minutes), and return {sessionId, resumed} or create a new one.
- Heartbeat: POST /api/sessions/[id]/heartbeat updates lastHeartbeatAt.
- A cron route marks stale sessions (>5 min, no heartbeat, no websocket) as 'disconnected', then 'abandoned' after the grace window.
- Adapter sends HELLO{installationId, agentId, projectId}; the server matches same agent+installation+project+recently-disconnected and offers resume vs new.

WHY THIS MATTERS TO THE USER (section 3.2 UI consequence): dead sessions must never make characters vanish. Claude offline shows Level/XP/wins plus 'Last seen 3m ago'; reopening flips to ONLINE with the SAME character. Session history doubles as a replayable game mechanic.

CONSIDERATIONS: the grace window is a real product decision (15 min default per section 22) - too short and an accidental terminal kill loses battle progress; too long and a genuinely abandoned session holds a slot. Make it configurable.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: kill a terminal mid-session, reopen, and get a resume offer rather than a duplicate agent; heartbeat keeps a session alive; the sweeper transitions disconnected -> abandoned on schedule.

TESTS: unit test for the state machine transitions; integration test that a HELLO within the grace window resumes the same sessionId and outside it creates a new one; test that sessions.agent_id is the only identity FK (no user_id identity column).
close_reason: CONTRACT 3. Pure state machine (active/ended/disconnected/abandoned) with an exhaustive transition matrix; disconnected is resumable, only ended+abandoned are terminal. HELLO handshake matches on agent+installation+project and can never create a character. Heartbeat staleness and the resume grace window are single-sourced helpers shared by the handshake and the sweeper. 24 unit tests + 25 integration tests against live Postgres. Found+fixed a 15-hour grace window from a units bug, and a missing unique index on projects that made every session non-resumable (migration 0002).

title: CONTRACT 4: Public API = Application Commands/Queries (single domain impl)
description:
Implement and FREEZE Contract 4: the Agent Protocol surface, per plan section 29.1 item 4, section 31, section 32, section 33, section 36.

THE PRINCIPLE (section 29.1 item 4): Application Commands and Queries are the SINGLE definition of what an agent can do. CLI / MCP / REST are CONSUMERS of it.

IRON RULE (section 31): the CLI contains ZERO game logic and touches NO DB. It calls the Public API only - the same claimQuest(agentId, questId) application command the web and MCP paths use. Future surfaces (Discord bot, GitHub App, SDK) reuse the same command and must NEVER reimplement per surface.

THE STABLE SURFACE (section 32) - frozen, about 5 primitives:
- discover([domain?]) - lazy catalog; top-level domains first; per-domain detail on demand; NEVER the full 200-capability firehose at connect.
- search({type, status, difficulty, ...})
- inspect({type, id})
- act({action, target, input})
- observe({scope})

THE PROBLEM THIS SOLVES: N features x M operations collapses to 100-200 MCP tools, which is undiscoverable and bloats agent context. The principle is 'cover every capability, expose few stable primitives'.

ANTI-GOD-TOOL GUARD (section 32): act() dispatches TYPED, REGISTRY-DEFINED actions - defineAction({id:'quest.claim', input: ClaimQuestInput, output: ClaimQuestResult, permissions}) - NEVER act({action: string, payload: any}). Type safety and discoverability must be preserved.

DOMAIN CAPABILITIES live in the REGISTRY, not as MCP tools: quest.list/claim/submit, battle.challenge/accept, guild.join/leave and so on. Feature growth must NOT equal surface growth: adding Guild changes the registry, not the 5 primitives.

THE CLI USES THE IDENTICAL ABSTRACTION (section 32): 'quest list' -> search(type=quest); 'quest claim <id>' -> act('quest.claim', ...).

ARCHITECTURE (section 33): CORE -> Extension Contract -> GAME extensions | INTERFACE extensions | INFRASTRUCTURE extensions.
- extensions/* declare capabilities and know NOTHING about MCP/CLI/REST/Web.
- interfaces/{cli,mcp,api,websocket}/* are capability CONSUMERS/adapters; adding a feature never edits them, only composition/manifest registration.
- infrastructure/* is integrations behind boundaries.

MACHINE-NATIVE ASSUMPTION (section 34): every gameplay loop must be fully playable through the protocol/tool interface alone, with no web clicks required. If a quest cannot be discovered -> claimed -> submitted -> rewarded via discover/search/act plus the CLI equivalents, the feature is NOT done.

FEATURE LAYOUT NOTE (section 33): features may gain an application/ directory holding command/query handlers (the single domain implementation all surfaces share). Default is pure registry entries with no per-feature interface code.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: one application command is reachable identically from CLI, HTTP, and MCP; act() is fully typed (a bogus action id is a compile error, not a runtime string); adding a feature adds registry entries and zero new primitives.

TESTS: a parity test asserting the same application command is invoked through each surface; a type-level test that an unknown action id fails to compile; a test that adding a dummy feature increases the registry but not the 5-primitive surface.

CONSIDERATIONS: this is the bead where 'expose little' has to become real. The pressure to add a convenient sixth primitive - or to promote quest.claim to a first-class tool because an agent asked for it - will arrive early and repeatedly. The plan's counter-argument should be the default: that operation already exists in the registry, and promoting it means every future feature will ask the same. The other risk is per-feature interface code creeping in; the review rule in section 36 is the guard, so encode it in the CI architecture check rather than relying on reviewers noticing.
close_reason: CONTRACT 4. packages/api is the single Application API: discover/search/inspect/act/observe, frozen at five. Parity test drives the same action through CLI-shaped, HTTP-shaped and MCP-shaped calls and asserts identical results and identical failures. Adding 7 features grows the registry 2->9 domains with no change to the surface, asserted on both the constant and the returned object's keys. Unknown actions name the known domains rather than dumping every id. Honest limit: action ids are runtime-registered by independently-built packages, so a bogus id is a typed runtime error rather than a compile error without codegen.

title: Capability registry + typed action definitions
description:
Build the capability registry and the typed action definition system that sits between the Extension API and every interface surface, per plan section 32 and section 33.

WHAT IT IS: A registry mapping capability names to the feature that provides them, plus a typed defineAction() helper for domain operations.

TWO REGISTRIES (section 20 registry.ts):
- command registry: command type -> CommandHandler (duplicate types throw at install)
- capability registry: capability name -> owning feature id

The GameFeature.capabilities[] array populates the capability registry at install. requires[] is validated against it, producing the degrade-with-warning path.

TYPED ACTIONS (section 32 Anti-God-Tool guard):
defineAction({ id: 'quest.claim', input: ClaimQuestInput, output: ClaimQuestResult, permissions })
The guard exists because act({action: string, payload: any}) destroys both type safety and discoverability. A bogus action id must be a COMPILE error, not a runtime surprise.

ID NAMING: dotted domain.operation, e.g. quest.list / quest.claim / quest.submit, battle.challenge / battle.accept, guild.join / guild.leave. These are REGISTRY capabilities, never MCP tool names - the plan is emphatic that historical domain-operation names (register_agent, get_world, get_quests, challenge_agent, accept_battle, send_message, claim_reward, spawn_agent...) describe capabilities in the registry and must NOT be implemented verbatim as MCP tools. That verbatim list is exactly the tool-explosion path the plan bans.

WHY THE REGISTRY IS THE INTEGRATION POINT (section 33): features declare capabilities; interfaces/{cli,mcp,api,websocket} consume them. Because of this, adding a feature never edits an interface implementation - it only adds a manifest/registry entry. That is the property the removal test and the architecture-failure review rule both depend on.

LAZY DISCOVERY (section 32 discover()): the catalog must return top-level domains first, with per-domain detail on demand. Never ship the full capability list at connect time - that is what bloats agent context.

CONSIDERATIONS: permission metadata on each action is how surfaces enforce authorization uniformly rather than each surface re-implementing authz. Wire it now; retrofitting it means auditing every action later.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: features register capabilities at install and deregister at uninstall; defineAction gives compile-time input/output typing; a feature's requires[] that is unsatisfied degrades with a warning naming the missing capability.

TESTS: unit test for register/deregister symmetry; type-level test that an unknown action id fails to compile; test that discover() returns domains before details (assert the lazy shape).
notes: BLOCKER for ba-mcp-adapter-li2, found 2026-09-24. The MCP spec (2026-07-28, server/tools) says a tool that declares an outputSchema MUST return structured content conforming to it, delivered via structuredContent. That makes the deferred codegen a blocker rather than a nice-to-have, the moment MCP begins: discover/search/inspect CAN declare honest static outputSchemas because their shapes are static, but act CANNOT, because the set of valid action ids is decided at runtime by independently built packages. act must therefore declare NO outputSchema, with a comment saying why; a permissive {type:'object'} would claim a guarantee the spec then reads as a MUST. The code fix is codegen emitting a union of every registered id with its input and output.

Verified with a probe: runAction takes the caller's own I and O, so with no contextual type the result is unknown, with one it is the caller's unchecked assertion, and a misspelled action id, a wrong input shape and a wrong expected output all compile clean. title: Activity/Event Log feature (P0) + persisted-event filter
description:
Implement the Activity/Event Log as a first-class P0 feature, per plan section 30 and the persistence filter in section 7.2.

WHY IT IS P0 AND NOT A DEBUG TABLE (section 29.4 + section 30): replay, audit, achievements, reputation, anti-abuse, and battle history ALL read from ONE ordered, attributed action trail. Paperclip treats action attribution the same way. Scattering this data across feature tables would mean each of those five consumers re-derives it differently.

THE TRAIL SHAPE (section 30), per session:
  Agent #123 / Session #456
  10:02 claim bounty -> 10:04 modify 3 files -> 10:07 run tests ->
  10:08 submit PR -> 10:11 PR merged -> 10:11 bounty completed -> +500 XP

IMPLEMENTATION:
- event_log table (section 21): id (bigserial), type, actorId, payload jsonb, occurredAt
- features/activity/ extension owning the append/query API and the retention policy
- every runtime.emit appends KEY events; transient telemetry stays on the bus only
- PERSISTED_EVENT_TYPES (section 21/22) = ['session.started','session.ended','test.passed','test.failed','bounty.claimed','bounty.completed','battle.started','battle.finished','agent.level_up'] - everything else goes to the SSE bus ONLY.

THE REASON FOR THE FILTER IS THE CORE BACKEND INSIGHT (section 7.2): coding agents emit torrents. 100 agents x 20 events/s = 2000 DB writes/s. Neon must NEVER see that. Architecture: Agents -> Next.js Event Gateway -> {Realtime layer (WS/SSE) -> Browser} + {batched/important -> Neon}. Realtime is NOT Neon's job.

ORDERING: the runtime emits in the order persist -> handlers -> publish. The log must be written before downstream consumers read it, or replay/achievements can race ahead of the durable record.

CONSIDERATIONS: retention policy is part of this feature's scope (section 30 says 'owns append/query API, retention policy'). Replays need old events, so retention cannot be aggressive; decide and document the window. Retention is also the natural pressure valve if event volume grows.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: every key event lands in event_log with actor and ordering; transient events (thinking, waiting, streaming, heartbeat) provably do NOT; replay, achievements, and reputation all read from this one log rather than from scattered feature tables.

TESTS: unit test that the persist filter admits exactly PERSISTED_EVENT_TYPES; integration test that ordering survives concurrent emits; test that querying a session's trail returns the example shape from section 30.
close_reason: features/activity owns the read API (trail + recent), the session summary shape, and the retention policy (365 days, because a shared replay is a link). Added the missing bridge: DrizzleStateStore, the only path an event takes to the database. 10 unit tests pin the persist filter (exactly the key events, features may add their own), retention boundaries and summary rendering; 34 integration tests prove key events land and transient ones provably do not, ordering survives, and prune removes only what aged out.

title: Better Auth + GitHub OAuth + local OAuth contract (M0)
description:
Set up Better Auth with GitHub OAuth over PostgreSQL, per plan sections 38 and 39. No hand-rolled OAuth.

WHY BETTER AUTH (section 38): Next.js-native (mounted at /api/auth/[...all]), GitHub OAuth built in, session management included, extensible later to passkey / API key / JWT / organizations / roles, and aligned with the MCP and agent-auth roadmap. The plan previously said 'GitHub OAuth' without naming a framework; this is the locked choice.

THE FLOW:
  Human -> GitHub OAuth -> Better Auth -> {User -> Agent extension -> Quest/Bounty/Progression/Battle/Guild
                                          Session (human web session; NOT agent session)}

HARD SEPARATION (section 38, enforce in review): Better Auth owns User / Auth / human-Session ONLY. The game domain stays in extensions. The GitHub OAuth token is NEVER agent identity.

LOCAL CONTRIBUTOR CONTRACT (section 39) - every contributor must get this green on a clean clone:
  127.0.0.1:3000 -> GitHub OAuth -> /api/auth/[...all]/callback -> local DB (container Postgres)
- GitHub OAuth App: homepage http://127.0.0.1:3000, callback http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/auth/callback/github. Document these EXACT URLs in .env.example comments, and note the localhost alias issue because GitHub matches callback URLs strictly (a common contributor failure: redirect_uri_mismatch).
- .env.example keys: BETTER_AUTH_SECRET, BETTER_AUTH_URL=http://127.0.0.1:3000, GITHUB_CLIENT_ID, GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET, DATABASE_URL (local container default; Neon branch URL for preview).
- First-login bootstrap: new GitHub user -> users row -> EMPTY agent list -> dashboard prompts CLI/MCP connect (section 4). No manual SQL.

FAILURE MODES to document in apps/web/README.md (section 39): wrong callback URL (GitHub error redirect_uri_mismatch), missing secret (Better Auth boot error), DB unreachable (migration/seed step missed, see the local-testing-contract bead).

M0 COMPOSITION (section 38, amends section 33 P0 list): Next.js, Postgres/Neon, Better Auth, GitHub OAuth, User identity, Agent identity, Agent credential, Agent session, Event Bus, Extension API, CLI, local Docker dev env.

ONBOARDING UX this enables (section 4): agentbattle.gg -> [Continue with GitHub] -> Dashboard 'Connect your Coding Agent' -> per-agent cards -> 'claude mcp add agent-battle <url>' -> browser auth -> terminal 'connected, you can now enter the arena'. One account fans out to multiple agents with no per-session GitHub re-login.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: from a clean clone, docker compose up + migrations + seed + GitHub login works at 127.0.0.1:3000; logout then login shows the same user and the same agents.

TESTS: an auth stub test that bypasses the real GitHub round trip for CI; integration test for the first-login bootstrap creating a users row with an empty agent list; a test asserting the human session is never used as agent identity.

CONSIDERATIONS: the callback-URL mismatch is the single most likely reason a newcomer's first run fails, because GitHub matches callback URLs strictly and localhost/127.0.0.1 are treated as different origins. Document the exact URLs in .env.example rather than a README nobody reads. Also resist letting Better Auth grow: section 38 is emphatic that it owns human auth ONLY, and every game concept that creeps into its config (agent tokens, session identity, progression) is a future extraction cost.

title: Docker Compose local dev: web + Postgres, offline-capable (M0)
description:
Make the project run with one command on a clean clone, per plan section 37.

THE LOCKED LOCAL CONTRACT: git clone -> cp .env.example .env -> docker compose up runs the app with HMR, OFFLINE (no Neon required).

WHY (section 37): Next.js + DB + CLI + MCP/worker later is too many moving parts to ask contributors to install Node and Postgres manually. This bead is a gap fill, NOT an architecture change.

LAYOUT per section 37:
  / (repo root)
  docker/Dockerfile, docker/Dockerfile.dev, .dockerignore
  compose.yaml, compose.dev.yaml, .env.example

M0 SERVICES: web (Next.js dev, bind-mount + Compose Watch/HMR) and postgres (local PG, named volume agent-battle-postgres-data, survives restarts). LATER and ONLY when needed: worker (background jobs), standalone MCP server, queue. Compose may also run lint/test parity services for CI/local sameness.

DB MODES: default local = container Postgres (offline-capable); cloud/preview = Neon branch per-developer/per-PR via neonctl link/checkout/env pull. NEON IS NEVER A LOCAL-RUN DEPENDENCY.

ARCHITECTURAL INVARIANT (section 37): Docker lives in the INFRASTRUCTURE layer. Features never import Docker/Compose/Postgres-container concepts - only repository and capability interfaces (section 33). The dependency-rules bead enforces this.

M0 DoD GAINS (section 37): docker compose up from a clean clone gets web + migrations + seed + CLI bootstrap all green; docker compose down && docker compose up preserves the local DB via the named volume.

NOTE ON THE OLDER PHRASING: section 7.1's earlier 'no Docker' phrasing is SUPERSEDED for local dev. Docker is the local development/test environment; it is never a PRODUCTION dependency. Production remains Vercel + Neon (git push deploys).

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a clean clone plus cp .env.example .env plus docker compose up yields a working app with HMR and a persistent DB, entirely offline.

TESTS: a smoke script that asserts compose config validity; a test that the named volume survives down/up; a test that docker-compose files do not leak into packages/features (the invariant above).

CONSIDERATIONS: the named volume is the whole point - a contributor who loses their local DB on every `docker compose down` will not trust the setup. Separately, resist adding services early: the plan adds worker/queue/MCP-split containers only when section 7.4 triggers. The temptation to compose a full production topology locally is strong and directly contradicts section 7.1's deploy-ease philosophy.
close_reason: Verified by running docker/scripts/smoke.sh: compose files parse, M0 services present (postgres/web/test-runner profile), no worker/queue/MCP containers added ahead of the scale-up trigger, postgres persists to the named volume agent-battle-postgres-data, no Docker/Compose concepts leak into apps/ or packages/, and data survives docker compose down && up. All six checks pass against a live stack.

title: Local testing contract: pnpm test:m0 canonical pipeline
description:
Establish the single canonical test pipeline that both local dev and CI run, per plan section 40. Docker Compose is the gate.

THE PIPELINE (section 40):
  docker compose up -> migrations -> seed -> unit (vitest) -> integration (+Postgres service) ->
  removal-test (section 20) -> license check (section 28.3) -> E2E smoke (login -> connect -> claim -> replay render)

RULES:
- compose.yaml services (M0): web, postgres, plus a test-runner profile for lint/unit/integration parity. Worker/queue/MCP-split containers only when section 7.4 triggers a scale-up.
- 'pnpm test:m0' runs the full chain locally; ANY step red blocks merge.
- The load test (100 agents x 20 events/s, section 7.2) stays a PRE-M4 GATE, not an M0 gate.

E2E SMOKE ASSERTIONS (section 40): the section 27 M0 DoD (login -> logout -> login shows the same user and agents) PLUS a GitHub-login stub -> agent HELLO -> bounty claim -> replay page renders, with the sandbox payout banner visible.

WHY CI RUNS THE SAME STEPS INSIDE THE SAME IMAGES (section 40): parity. A test that passes locally and fails in CI (or vice versa) wastes more contributor time than it saves. 'Compose may also run lint/test parity services for CI/local sameness' is the mechanism.

CONSIDERATIONS: the pipeline must be resumable/parallel where safe (unit tests are fast and independent; integration needs Postgres). Keep the ordering explicit so a failure message says which stage failed. Secrets for the GitHub stub must be test-only and never touch real OAuth credentials.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: pnpm test:m0 runs every stage in order and reports which stage failed; CI invokes the same script in the same images; a red stage blocks merge.

TESTS: the pipeline itself; plus a test that asserts each stage is invoked (e.g. a stage marker file written per stage) so stages cannot be silently skipped.

title: CLI agent-battle: P0 foundation, zero game logic, no DB
description:
Ship the agent-battle CLI in P0 alongside the API, per plan section 31, corrected by section 36.

WHY P0 AND NOT LATER TOOLING (section 31): the CLI is the agent's DAILY RUNTIME ENTRY POINT, not developer convenience. Section 33 explicitly reverses the earlier 'MCP-first, CLI-follows' reading - MCP does NOT have to be P0. Protocol/API + CLI ship first; MCP is an adapter on the SAME protocol later. This keeps the core cleaner and is Pi-consistent.

THE IRON RULE (section 31): the CLI contains ZERO game logic and touches NO DB. It calls the Public API only - the same claimQuest(agentId, questId) application command the web and MCP paths use. Future surfaces (Discord bot, GitHub App, SDK) reuse the same command and must NEVER reimplement it per surface.

ARCHITECTURE (section 31):
  Web App (Next.js) -+
                       +-> Public API -> Core Runtime -> Extensions -> Neon
  CLI (agent-battle) --+

THREE CLI ROLES:
1. AGENT RUNTIME: login / init / start / status / stop
2. PLATFORM INTERACTION: agent status, quest list/claim, bounty list/inspect, profile, xp, submit
3. DEV/ADMIN: dev, doctor, config, extension

LAYOUT per section 31, packages/cli/: src/commands/{login,init,start,status,stop,agent,quest,bounty,profile,dev,doctor,config,extension}, runtime/local.ts, api-client.ts. Thin wrappers over the Application API (contract-public-api), argparse-only, NO domain imports.

AgentRuntime abstraction (start/stop/status/send) with future LocalCliRuntime / McpRuntime / RemoteRuntime / EmbeddedRuntime. A CLI restart creates a NEW SESSION but the SAME Agent ID (section 3.2).

SURFACE PARITY (section 32): the CLI uses the identical capability abstraction as every other surface - 'quest list' is search(type=quest); 'quest claim <id>' is act('quest.claim', ...). CLI and MCP evolve INDEPENDENTLY of feature count: adding Guild changes the registry, not the CLI or the primitives.

REVIEW GUARD (section 36): any PR adding interfaces/cli/* implementation code FOR A SPECIFIC GAME FEATURE (instead of registry entries) fails review. The CLI must not grow per-feature branches.

AGENT-FRIENDLY UX: this is an agent-facing CLI, so it should also support non-interactive/robot modes, clear actionable errors, and layered help. Consider a --json output mode for machine consumption, since agents will drive it.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: 'agent-battle login/init/start/status/stop' works against the API; a quest can be listed and claimed entirely from the CLI; no DB connection and no domain import exists anywhere under packages/cli/.

TESTS: CLI integration tests against a live API in the compose test environment; an architecture test that greps packages/cli/ for forbidden DB/domain imports; a test that the same quest claim via CLI and via HTTP produces identical application-command effects.

CONSIDERATIONS: the hardest part of this bead is restraint. It is tempting to give the CLI convenient shortcuts - a --with-xp flag, a local cache of bounties, a direct DB read for speed. Each one is an iron-rule violation that will make the CLI behave differently from the web and MCP surfaces. Also: the CLI is the surface an AGENT will drive, not only a human, so it should support non-interactive and machine-readable output (a --json mode and actionable errors) from the start. Retrying that later means auditing every command.

title: Agent credential issuance, rotation, scopes, expiry
description:
Implement agent credential lifecycle: issuance, rotation, revocation, scopes, and expiry, per plan sections 21, 29.1, 31, and 34.

SCHEMA (section 21): agent_credentials: id, installationId -> installations, tokenHash, scopes jsonb, expiresAt, revokedAt, createdAt.

HARD RULES:
- Store a HASH, never the raw token (section 38).
- Issuance/rotation endpoints live under the AGENT EXTENSION, not inside Better Auth config (section 38). Better Auth owns human auth only.
- A token authenticates a user/installation and NEVER equals a session (section 3.4).

TEMPORARY IDENTITY TOKENS (section 3.5 and 13.2, from the Moltbook pattern - NOTE: section 29 flags Moltbook details as UNVERIFIED hypothesis, so keep the PRINCIPLE and drop citation certainty): adopt temporary identity tokens (1h expiry, minted from a permanent key) to separate Permanent Identity / Credential / Session / Event IDs. The separation of these four ID classes is the sound, independently-justified part.

TOKEN LEAKAGE (section 3.4): NEVER put raw tokens in MCP URLs. The plan's own bad example is https://agentbattle.gg/mcp?token=xxxx because tokens in URLs leak into logs and browser history. Use MCP OAuth -> short-lived access tokens. Web GitHub login and MCP agent authorization are related but SEPARATE credentials - do not reuse one raw credential for both.

SCOPES: agent_credentials.scopes drives the permissions field on defineAction (capability-registry), so authorization is enforced uniformly across CLI/MCP/API rather than re-implemented per surface.

ROTATION: support rotation without downtime if possible, and immediate revocation. Revoked credentials must fail cleanly with an actionable error, not a confusing 500.

CONSIDERATIONS: the 1h temporary-token lifetime is a real tradeoff - long enough that an active coding session does not churn, short enough that a leaked token has limited blast radius. Make it configurable.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: issue a credential, use it to authenticate, rotate it, then confirm the old one is rejected and the new one works; a revoked credential is rejected; raw tokens never appear in the database.

TESTS: unit test that issuance stores only a hash; integration test for issue/use/rotate/revoke; a test that a token in a URL is rejected by the auth layer (defense in depth); a test that expired temporary tokens are refused.
close_reason: SHA-256 over 32 CSPRNG bytes (full entropy, so no password KDF), constant-time comparison, 1h configurable lifetime. Raw token never stored — the integration test reads the whole row as text and asserts the token is absent. Rotation without downtime (replacement issued before the old is revoked, with a test for the exclusion that makes that true), immediate revocation via revoked_at rather than deletion, scope enforcement naming the missing scope. Tokens in URLs are refused by the auth layer, headers still honoured when both are present.

title: AgentEvent union + zod schemas + PROTOCOL_VERSION pin
description:
Define the versioned normalized event vocabulary that the entire game core speaks, per plan sections 5.2 and 20.

THE TAXONOMY (section 5.2) is the game core's ONLY vocabulary. The game NEVER knows Claude vs Codex vs OpenCode. SessionStarted/Stopped, PromptSubmitted, ToolStarted/Completed/Failed, FileRead/FileWrite, CommandRun, TestPassed/Failed, Thinking/Waiting, MessageSent/Received, SubagentSpawned/Completed, PermissionRequested, FileChanged, TaskCreated.

CONVERGED PATTERN FROM ALL RESEARCHED REPOS (section 1.2 conclusion): Agent -> normalized events -> State/GameEngine/Control split -> World. Adapters translate Claude hooks / Codex JSONL / OpenCode SQLite / pi events into one AgentEvent union, THEN the game decides mappings: FileWrite -> Workshop, CommandRun -> Terminal, Search -> Library, Message -> Comms room, Task -> quest, Spawn -> summon NPC, Tokens -> resource. AgentMove and Agent Quest both prove this taxonomy works across Claude/Codex/OpenCode/pi/Cursor/Copilot.

FILE: packages/protocol/src/agent-event.ts with PROTOCOL_VERSION = '0.1.0' and a zod discriminated union on 'type'. Section 20 provides the concrete shape - session.started, session.heartbeat, session.ended, tool.started, tool.completed, file.read, file.write, command.run, test.passed, test.failed, thinking, waiting, permission.requested, message.sent, subagent.spawned, subagent.completed - each carrying sessionId and at (plus type-specific fields such as harness enum, exitCode, linesAdded/linesRemoved).

ALSO: packages/protocol/schemas/*.json for cross-language adapters, and packages/protocol/src/version.ts.

VERSION PIN IS A RISK CONTROL (section 17.3): keep the AgentEvent union versioned (skill.json-style pin) so adapter PRs from third parties do not break core. Section 33 P3 requires version-checking on every handshake with a warning and changelog link on mismatch.

CONSIDERATIONS: the union is the contract between third-party adapters and our core, so it must stay small and stable. Prefer adding a new event type over overloading an existing one with optional fields - overloads make consumer switches ambiguous.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: every taxonomy item from section 5.2 has a zod schema and a TS type; validation rejects malformed events with a useful message; PROTOCOL_VERSION is exported and checked at handshake.

TESTS: round-trip validation tests per event type; a test that an unknown event type is rejected; a snapshot test that locks the union shape so an accidental breaking change fails CI.
close_reason: All 21 section 5.2 taxonomy events now have zod schemas + TS types (added prompt.submitted, tool.failed, file.changed, message.received, task.created). Validation rejects malformed with field-level messages; unknown types name every known type. PROTOCOL_VERSION exported, pinned in the JSON Schema , checked in the artifact test. 9 protocol tests incl. a compile-time exhaustiveness check and a shape snapshot.

title: Port TOOL_NAME_MAP / TOOL_ZONE_MAP normalization from agent-move
description:
Port the tool normalization layer from agent-move into packages/protocol/src/tool-map.ts, per plan section 28.1 item 2 and section 20.

SOURCE: .tmp/agent-move/packages/shared/src/constants/tools.ts - 157 lines, MIT licensed, containing TOOL_NAME_MAP (~50 entries), TOOL_ZONE_MAP, normalizeToolName(), and getZoneForTool(). Also port zones.ts, colors.ts, names.ts from the same directory as naming seeds.

WHY THIS IS A DIRECT COPY (section 28.1 item 2): agent-move is the single best-documented reference for normalizing many CLIs into one vocabulary. Section 1.2 item 4 calls it a 'textbook' implementation and says STEAL: copy the AgentWatcher + normalization VERBATIM as our adapters/ template. The plan explicitly classifies this as a copy-with-attribution, not a rewrite.

EXTEND THE ZONE SET: add bounty-board, battle-arena, guild-hall alongside the existing Files/Terminal/Search/Web/Thinking/Messaging/Tasks/Spawn/Idle, so the game client can map tools to our world (section 20, section 25).

ATTRIBUTION REQUIREMENT: keep the original copyright header (MIT) and add a THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md entry naming agent-move, the file, and the commit SHA (section 28.3). The license-hygiene bead's CI check enforces this.

CONSIDERATIONS: ~50 tool entries will go stale as harnesses add tools. normalizeToolName() should degrade gracefully to a sensible default zone for unknown tools rather than dropping the event - an unmapped tool is still real activity and should not break the pipeline.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: normalizeToolName maps the known harnesses' tool names to canonical names; getZoneForTool returns a zone for every canonical tool including the new bounty/battle/guild zones; unknown tools return a default rather than throwing.

TESTS: a table-driven unit test over the mapping; a test that every canonical tool resolves to a valid zone; a test that an unknown tool degrades gracefully; a test asserting the attribution header survived the port.

title: features/agent: identity, HELLO, heartbeat, presence
description:
Build the agent extension - the first game feature, per plan section 24.

COMMANDS: RegisterAgent, HelloSession, Heartbeat, EndSession.
EVENTS: agent.registered, session.started / session.resumed / session.ended.
OWNERS: writes to agents / sessions / installations tables only (section 29.4 persistence split: users/agents/agent_credentials/sessions/event_log are platform-owned; feature-owned tables are bounties/quests/progressions/reputations/battles/guilds).

MACHINE-NATIVE FROM BIRTH (section 33 P1 rule): this feature must expose CLI/MCP-consumable capabilities FROM THE START - design machine-native, never 'game first, protocol later'. Registering an agent and running a session must be fully drivable through the 5 stable primitives and the CLI.

THE IDENTITY RESOLUTION LOGIC lives here: given HELLO{installationId, agentId, projectId} plus harness and project repo URL, find-or-create installation, agent, and project, then locate a recently-disconnected session in the same agent+installation+project within the grace window and resume it (section 3.2, section 22). Do NOT key on process name alone - three concurrent Claudes must stay distinguishable.

PRESENCE: the agent row's status field moves ACTIVE -> OFFLINE on session end while all stats persist (section 3.2). The UI consequence: a dead session must never make the character vanish; offline shows Level/XP/wins plus 'Last seen 3m ago'.

CONSIDERATIONS: presence detection quality is a separate concern - see the status-fusion bead. This feature owns the state machine; the fusion bead owns inferring working/idle/attention/error from transcripts and pane text.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: an agent registers via the CLI, runs a session, heartbeats, ends cleanly, and shows offline with intact stats; a reconnect within the grace window resumes the session rather than duplicating the agent.

TESTS: unit tests for the session state machine; integration test for register -> hello -> heartbeat -> end; the kill-and-reopen resume test from the section 3.2 narrative (terminal killed mid-session, reopened, resume offered); test that agent stats survive session end.

title: Status fusion: pane + transcript -> idle/working/attention/error
description:
Port the status-fusion logic from arcane-agents into the agent extension's presence detector, per plan section 28.1 item 5 and section 1.2 item 5.

SOURCE: .tmp/arcane-agents/src/server/status/decide.ts - 1061 lines, MIT. It fuses pane text plus transcript into a small status set: idle / working / attention / error / stopped.

WHY: Section 1.2 item 5 calls this a concrete STEAL: 'status fusion, control-group UX for parties, SQLite schema draft.' Raw tool events tell you an agent is active, but not whether it is blocked on a PERMISSION PROMPT (attention) or has actually errored. That distinction is what makes a character legible in the world and what surfaces a permission queue as a real game mechanic (section 1.1 credits codemoo/agent-world with 'permission-queue-as-game-mechanic').

PORT THE LOGIC, NOT THE FRAMEWORK (section 28.1 item 5 wording: 'port logic (not framework)'). The source is Express/node-pty/tmux-oriented; our target is a pure function over event streams, so do not drag the framework along.

ALSO STEAL FROM THE SAME REPO: the SQLite schema as a Neon draft (section 1.2 item 5), and the RTS control-group UX for parties (section 1.2 item 5) - the party UX belongs to the guild/social beads, but the schema draft informs our session tables.

DO NOT (section 1.2 item 5 AVOID): tmux as a CORE dependency - keep it as one adapter backend only; Express/Canvas (use Next.js/PixiJS); the local-only assumption.

CONSIDERATIONS: the 1061-line source is the single largest ported file in the plan. Consider extracting the decision rules into a pure, table-driven module with its own tests rather than a direct transliteration, so the logic is auditable. agent-move's 30s idle timeout (section 1.2 item 4) is a useful complementary rule.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: given a fixture event stream, the detector produces the expected status transitions; 'attention' is raised on permission.requested and cleared on the corresponding resolution; no tmux or Express dependency leaks in.

TESTS: table-driven unit tests over representative event sequences (idle, working, permission-blocked, error, stopped); an architecture test asserting no tmux/Express import in packages/features/agent.

title: features/quest: generic quest CRUD, GitHub-linked or internal
description:
Implement the quest feature per plan section 24, the generic task unit that bounties build on.

SCOPE: generic quest CRUD, either GitHub-linked or internal. A quest has objective, progress, prerequisites, reward, difficulty, and a time limit (section 10.4 mechanics, informed by the Roblox quest-design reference the plan cites).

SCHEMA (section 21): quests: id, projectId -> projects, title, body, difficulty (default 1), xpReward (default 100), status (default 'open'), createdAt.

STRUCTURE: every packages/features/<name>/ ships domain.ts, commands.ts, events.ts, reducer.ts, rules.ts, repository.ts (drizzle access, own tables only), index.ts exporting a GameFeature, README.md listing capabilities, and *.test.ts (section 24).

MACHINE-NATIVE (section 33 P1 + section 34): a quest must be fully discoverable, claimable, submittable, and completable through discover/search/act and the CLI equivalents with NO web clicks. If a quest cannot be driven end-to-end via the protocol, the feature is not done.

QUEST IS NOT BOUNTY: a quest is the generic task unit; a bounty is a FUNDED quest backed by a real GitHub issue and real money (section 11.1, Appendix B). Keep them separate features - quest must work with no bounty extension installed (that is the removal-test proof).

CONSIDERATIONS: quest chains and campaigns (a project becoming an RPG campaign, section 10.4's Coding Quests shape) are listed under bounty chains in section 11.3, so link quests there rather than overloading this feature.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: quests can be created, listed, searched, claimed, progressed, and completed entirely via CLI/protocol; completing a quest emits a quest.completed event that other features may react to without importing quest internals.

TESTS: unit tests for the reducer; integration test for the full lifecycle over the API; a removal test that uninstalling quest leaves the runtime green; a machine-native test proving no step requires a web UI.

title: features/progression: XP, level, skills, builds (model != class)
description:
Implement the progression extension per plan sections 10.1, 10.2, and 24.

SUBSCRIBES: bounty.completed (main XP table), test.passed (small), battle.finished (win bonus). EMITS: agent.level_up.

LEVEL CURVE (section 24): xpForLevel(n) = 100 * n * (n+1) / 2, to be tuned later. Keep the formula in rules.ts as data, not inline logic, so tuning does not require touching the reducer.

XP FROM ACTUAL WORK, NEVER TOKENS (sections 10.2, 10.3, 17): PR merged +500, tests +100, recovery +150, bounty +1000. NOT tokens and NOT tool-call counts. Section 10.2 is explicit: 'XP from actual work - never tokens/tool-counts.' This is a core integrity property - a token-based economy would reward spamming.

MODEL IS NOT CLASS (section 10.2, the most important design idea in the progression system): class/build is derived from BEHAVIOR, not from the model name. The same Claude can be a Debugger in one project and a Researcher in another. Behavior->build classifiers live in rules.ts, NOT hardcoded per model (section 24).

THE TRIPLE SPLIT (section 10.2) - never conflate these:
- XP: progression toward Level
- Reputation: social and economic trust
- Stats: FACTS (127 PRs opened, 92 merged, 21 rejected, 14 abandoned)

RUNE SCAPE MODEL FITS BEST (section 10.2): independent skills (Coding, Debugging, Testing, Research, Refactoring, Security, Documentation, Collaboration) each with their own level per agent. There is NO single power scalar.

EVE INSIGHT: specialization without maxing everything (section 10.2). Level equals ACCESS, not cosmetics - level-gated content (Lv1 basic, Lv5 advanced, Lv10 Arena, Lv15 teams, Lv20 guild creation, Lv30 sponsoring).

DEATH RULE (section 10.2): HP 0 NEVER kills the character; only the SESSION fails. The agent lives, keeps its history, and still gains experience. Failure achievements are included. This protects the persistent-character premise from section 3.1.

MVP CHARACTER SHEET (section 10.2): Identity + XP/Level + Skills + Build + Reputation + Achievements + History. Equipment, cosmetics, pets, mounts, base, and guild come later - scope discipline (section 17.8).

CONSIDERATIONS: the behavior->build classifier is the piece most likely to need iteration; expose its weights as configuration and log the classification so a surprising result is debuggable rather than mysterious.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: two behavior histories on the same model produce two DIFFERENT builds (this is the section 27 M3 DoD); XP is awarded from real outcomes only; level gates actually gate content.

TESTS: unit test for the level curve and XP awards; the M3 DoD test (same model, two behavior histories, two builds); a test asserting no token-derived XP exists anywhere; a test that a failed session grants experience but does not delete the character.

title: features/reputation: trust from outcomes + bounty tier gating
description:
Implement the reputation extension per plan sections 10.2, 11.3, and 24.

SUBSCRIBES: bounty.completed / bounty.failed, battle.finished. Trust is a function of merged rate, acceptance rate, and review outcomes.

REPUTATION MUST BE COMPUTED FROM REAL OUTCOMES (section 11.3): '47 bounties done, $8,420 earned, 91% acceptance, 4.7 average review -> 8,921 reputation.' The plan is explicit that these numbers must be derived from ACTUAL GitHub/bounty outcomes, NOT self-assessed by the game. A reputation system that games can inflate is worthless as a trust signal.

TIER GATING (section 11.3) - reputation gates which bounties an agent may attempt:
- Beginner: $5-25, docs and small bugs
- Intermediate: $25-200, feature/bugfix
- Advanced: $200-1000, architecture and complex bugs
- Legendary: $1000+, major OSS contribution
Newcomers grind easy bounties upward. This is the progression-gating role reputation plays, distinct from progression-level gating.

REPUTATION IS TRUST, NOT PROGRESSION (section 10.2 triple split): XP/Level is progression; Reputation is social and economic trust; Stats are facts. Do not let reputation feed the level curve.

THIS FEATURE IS A CAPABILITY PROVIDER (section 24): it exposes reputation.read, which the battle feature declares in requires: ['reputation.read'] (section 24). That declared dependency is exactly what makes the battle degradation path and the removal test meaningful - when reputation is uninstalled, battles degrade to open rather than crash.

CONSIDERATIONS: the plan notes GitHub's own security bounty reward guidelines span hundreds to thousands by severity, but explicitly says those are specific to GitHub's security program and NOT general OSS bounty rates. Do not present our tiers as authoritative market rates.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: reputation updates from real bounty/battle outcomes; tier gates block and admit correctly; uninstalling reputation makes battle degrade with a warning instead of failing.

TESTS: unit tests for the trust formula; tier-boundary tests at each edge; a removal test asserting battle still runs (degraded) with reputation uninstalled; a test that reputation never contributes to XP.

title: features/bounty: M2 vertical slice - Issue to payout
description:
Implement the bounty extension - M2, the plan's most important slice. Per plan sections 11.1, 22, 24, 27.

M2 IS THE PROOF OF THE WHOLE IDEA (section 15.3): the three milestones that prove the project are M1, M2, and M4, and M2 is explicitly 'valuable with zero game UI' (section 15.1). Ship real utility BEFORE heavy game art (section 17.1: gimmick risk, ship M2 first). The M2 DoD (section 27, LOCKED): FIRST REAL GAME LOOP = full Bounty vertical slice: Issue -> Bounty -> Discover -> Claim -> Coding -> PR -> Review -> Merge -> Reward -> Activity/History. 'Reward is the payoff at the END of the first playable loop, never the first feature.'

THE BOUNTY OBJECT (section 11.1):
type Bounty = { id, repository{owner,name,url}, issue{number,url}, reward{amount,currency}, requirements[], status: open|claimed|submitted|review|paid|expired, sponsor{githubUserId} }

COMMANDS (section 24): CreateBounty, ClaimBounty, SubmitBounty, FundBounty, ExpireBounty.
EVENTS: bounty.created, bounty.claimed, bounty.submitted, bounty.completed (and bounty.failed for the reputation consumer).
OWNERS: bounties and bounty_funds tables only.

API FLOW (section 22):
- POST /api/bounties - create; validates the GitHub issue exists via Octokit; emits bounty.created
- POST /api/bounties/[id]/claim - agent session claims; emits bounty.claimed; sets claimedAgentId; RACE MODE REJECTS SECOND CLAIMS
- POST /api/bounties/[id]/submit - {prUrl} -> bounty.submitted
- POST /api/webhooks/github - PR merge -> bounty.completed -> progression/reputation/achievement handlers fire -> payout job enqueued

THE CORE INSIGHT (section 11.1): do NOT invent a fake issue system. The Bounty has REAL GitHub links - repository url, issue number, issue url. Game is the discovery/execution/reputation/visualization layer ON TOP of GitHub, not a replacement for it. Precedents cited: Tari public bounties repo (browse -> pick -> fork -> PR -> first merged wins) and the AsyncAPI rounds model (budget rounds, public amounts, resolution rates -> our Season model).

Bounty IS a FUNDED QUEST, and must remain a separate feature from quest (Appendix B: 'Bounty = funded quest on a real GitHub issue'). Bounty must work if quest is removed.

MACHINE-NATIVE (section 33 P1 / section 34): the full loop discover -> claim -> code -> submit -> reward must be drivable via the 5 stable primitives and the CLI with no web clicks.

CONSIDERATIONS: the payout rail is a separate bead (see payout-rail-dispute) because real-money compliance is unresolved (section 17.5). M2's DoD ships with a real-money rail STUBBED - record intent, no real payout - and the UI must clearly mark 'payout: manual/sandbox' (section 27). Do not let this bead quietly become a payment system.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: on a scratch repository, end to end - create a bounty on a real issue, claim it from an agent via the protocol, open a PR, merge it, the webhook completes the bounty, XP/reputation fire, and history shows the trail.

TESTS: the full vertical-slice integration test on a scratch repo; unit tests for the state machine including RACE-mode double-claim rejection; a removal test that bounty works with quest uninstalled; a test asserting the bounty carries real GitHub URLs rather than synthetic ones.

BOUNDARY WITH THE SIBLING BOUNDS BEADS (avoid double-implementation):
This bead owns the CORE BOUNTY LIFECYCLE ONLY - the Bounty object, its state machine (open -> claimed -> submitted -> review -> paid/expired), and the commands CreateBounty, ClaimBounty, SubmitBounty, FundBounty, ExpireBounty.
It does NOT own: the mode and tier taxonomy, quest chains, or seasons. Those belong to the bounty-modes-tiers-seasons bead.
CONCRETELY: this bead stores a 'mode' field and enforces RACE-mode double-claim rejection, because the lifecycle cannot be correct without it. The enum of valid modes, the tier thresholds, chain prerequisite logic, and season accounting are all in the sibling bead. If both beads try to define the mode enum, that is a duplication bug - one owns it.
This bead also does NOT own payout mechanics (see payout-rail-dispute) or the GitHub API client (see github-infrastructure) - it consumes both as dependencies.

title: Bounty open funding: multi-sponsor stacking
description:
Allow ANYONE - not just the repository owner - to fund or add to any public issue's bounty, per plan section 11.2.

THE MECHANIC: Alice creates a $200 bounty on her repo's issue #381. Bob, who does not own the repo, adds $50. Carol adds $100. The bounty total becomes $350, with each contribution tracked as a separate fund record.

SCHEMA SUPPORT: bounty_funds: id, bountyId -> bounties, sponsorUserId -> users, amountCents, createdAt. A bounty can have N fund rows; the displayed amount is their sum.

PRECEDENTS (section 11.2): Bountysource allowed multiple people to co-fund a single bounty for the same issue. BountyHub permits any third party to attach a bounty to a public GitHub issue, with payout after the PR is approved.

WHY THIS IS A PRODUCT PILLAR (section 11.2 + section 11.4): it makes BOTH Sponsor and Solver first-class players.
- SPONSOR: create, fund, set requirements, review PRs, award rewards
- SOLVER: discover, claim, code, submit, earn, level up
A person can be both. This is what turns a task list into an economy, and it is the mechanism behind 'Anyone can put a bounty on real GitHub work. Any coding agent can compete to solve it.'

COMMAND: FundBounty (already declared by the bounty feature; this bead adds the open-funding path and the authorization rule).

AUTHORIZATION: funding a bounty on someone else's repository must be permitted, but claiming/submitting must still be validated against real GitHub state.

CONSIDERATIONS: refund and dispute semantics become real once third parties contribute. At minimum, an expired or cancelled bounty must not silently swallow funds - decide and document the disposition. This interfaces with the payout-rail-dispute bead.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: three users can stack funds on one bounty and the total reflects all contributions; a non-owner can fund; per-sponsor attribution is preserved for payout.

TESTS: integration test for the stacked-funding scenario end to end; a test that the total is the sum of funds (not a stored scalar that can drift); an authorization test that a non-owner may fund but a random user may not award someone else's bounty.

title: Bounty modes, chains, and seasons
description:
Implement the bounty variety layer per plan section 11.3: competition modes, skill tiers, quest chains, guild treasuries, and seasons.

MODES (section 11.3):
- RACE: many agents, FIRST VALID PR WINS (Tari precedent)
- OPEN: many agents, maintainer chooses
- TOURNAMENT: same issue, best validated solution
- TEAM: role-composed team, ONE PR

TIERS (section 11.3, gated by skill/reputation - see feature-reputation): Beginner $5-25 / Intermediate $25-200 / Advanced $200-1000 / Legendary $1000+.

CHAINS (section 11.3, the strongest game hook in this section): linked bounties turn a repository's issue graph into an RPG CAMPAIGN. $100 auth -> $250 OAuth -> $500 SSO -> $2000 overhaul, each requiring the previous. Render the GitHub issue tree as a quest tree, with reward, difficulty, sponsor, claimer, and progress per node. GitHub becomes the quest database.

GUILD TREASURIES: guilds fund collectively (section 11.3).

SEASONS (section 11.3): a time-boxed bounty round, e.g. 'Season 1: Open Source Bounty Hunt', with monthly pools and leaderboards. Precedent: the AsyncAPI bounty program (budget rounds, public amounts, resolution rates).

ECONOMY DISCIPLINE (section 11, section 10.4): XP, Coins, Reputation, Items, Cosmetics ONLY. NO crypto, NO NFT. Real money and game progression stay SEPARATE - never represent money as XP or vice versa. Mappings: quest -> XP, win -> Reputation, achievement -> Badge, season -> Cosmetic, guild contribution -> Guild XP.

SCOPE NOTE (section 17.8): seasons and tournaments are NOT in the M0-M4 MVP. This bead is P1-adjacent groundwork; the fully playable season system belongs to M6/M7. Build the data model and the mode enum now so early bounties carry the right shape, but do not build season UI here.

CONSIDERATIONS: the bounty must carry a mode field from creation, because RACE-mode double-claim rejection in the bounty feature depends on it. Introducing modes later would require a migration of live bounties.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a bounty carries a mode and a tier; RACE mode rejects a second claim while OPEN mode permits multiple; chains render as a tree with prerequisites enforced; no crypto anywhere in the schema or code.

TESTS: table-driven tests over the four modes; tier-boundary tests; a chain-prerequisite test (a $500 SSO bounty is not claimable until the $250 OAuth bounty completes); a grep-level test asserting no crypto/NFT code paths exist.

title: Payout rail + dispute path for real-money bounties (design before promising)
description:
DESIGN (and stub) the payout rail and dispute path for real-money bounties. This is the unresolved blocker flagged in plan section 17.5, and it must be settled BEFORE the product ever promises real amounts.

THE OPEN RISK (section 17.5): 'Payment/compliance for real-money bounties: M2 needs payout rail + dispute path design (not yet specified in conversation - must design before promising amounts).' The conversation never settled this. It is a genuine gap, and the plan correctly says so.

M2 SCOPE (section 27): the DoD ships with real money STUBBED - 'record intent, no real payout until section 17.5 resolved - mark clearly in UI payout: manual/sandbox.' The UI banner is a hard requirement, not a nicety: users must never believe they have been paid when they have not.

WHAT THIS BEAD MUST PRODUCE:
1. A payout rail decision: which provider(s), escrow vs direct transfer, KYC/AML posture, tax/reporting obligations, minimum bounty size, refund policy.
2. A dispute path: who adjudicates, what evidence is required (the activity log is the audit trail - section 30), time limits, refund to multiple co-sponsors when a bounty is cancelled or a maintainer rejects a valid PR.
3. A compliance checklist: what legal exposure does accepting money for OSS work create, and at what scale does it require counsel.
4. A stub interface so the bounty feature records payout INTENT (bounty_funded -> payout_pending -> payout_recorded) without moving money.

WHY THE ACTIVITY LOG MATTERS HERE: section 30 lists audit and anti-abuse as reasons the ordered, attributed event trail exists. A dispute is resolved by replaying what actually happened, so the log must be sufficient evidence. If the log cannot settle a dispute, the design is incomplete.

CONSIDERATIONS: the refund-on-cancel case is the hardest, because open funding (bounty-open-funding) means multiple sponsors with different expectations. Decide proportional refund semantics.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a written design exists and is referenced from the bounty feature; the stub interface records intent with no money movement; the sandbox banner is present and tested; nothing in the product claims a real payout.

TESTS: test that a completed bounty records payout intent in the correct state; test that the sandbox banner renders whenever a bounty is in a paid-adjacent state; a test that the payout stub cannot be invoked in a mode that implies real transfer.

title: Achievements (incl. failure achievements) driven by the activity log
description:
Implement achievements as a feature reading from the activity log, per plan sections 10.2, 21, 24, and 30.

SCHEMA (section 21): achievements: id, agentId -> agents, code, awardedAt.

ACHIEVEMENTS ARE EVENT-DERIVED, NOT SCRIPTED (section 30): replay, achievements, reputation, and audit all read from the ONE ordered activity log, never from scattered feature tables. An achievement is therefore a projection over the event stream - which means achievements become retroactively grantable if a rule is added later (decide and document whether backfill is allowed; granting a missed 'first bounty' badge to an established agent is arguably correct).

EXAMPLES from the plan's own vocabulary: 'First Bounty' (section 12.2 cites progression reacting to bounty.completed with an achievement check), and FAILURE ACHIEVEMENTS (section 10.2) - the plan explicitly includes achievements for failure. This is consistent with the death rule: HP 0 never kills the character, only the session fails, and failure is itself a recordable accomplishment (e.g. recovering from five failed attempts is a 'critical hit', not a shame).

MACHINE-NATIVE (section 33/34): achievements must be readable and awardable through the protocol and CLI, not only rendered in a web page.

CONSIDERATIONS: achievement codes should be stable, versioned strings (like the protocol version pin in section 17.3) so a renamed achievement does not orphan historical rows.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: completing a first bounty awards the matching code exactly once; a failure-path achievement can be earned; achievements are derived from the log rather than from feature-table joins.

TESTS: unit test that an award is idempotent (never double-awarded); a test that a failure-path achievement is grantable; a test that achievements derive from event_log and not from a feature table.

title: GitHub infrastructure: webhooks, issue validation, PR merge detection
description:
Build the GitHub integration behind the infrastructure boundary, per plan sections 19, 22, and 33.

COMPONENTS:
- POST /api/webhooks/github: issues and PRs become quests/bounties; a PR merge completes a bounty (section 22). Signature verification is mandatory - an unauthenticated webhook endpoint that can mint XP is a trivial exploit.
- Issue existence validation via Octokit when a bounty is created (section 22): POST /api/bounties 'validates GitHub issue exists via Octokit'.
- PR merge detection driving bounty.completed.

ARCHITECTURAL PLACEMENT (section 33): infrastructure/* is an INTEGRATION BEHIND A BOUNDARY. The bounty feature does not import Octokit or know GitHub's API shape - it consumes events and issues commands. This keeps the feature testable without the network and keeps a GitHub outage from corrupting game state.

REALITY: GitHub is BOTH authentication and quest source (section 3.3). It authenticates humans and supplies repos/issues/PRs, but it does NOT identify local agents. That separation is a hard invariant (see contract-agent-identity).

CONSIDERATIONS: webhooks are at-least-once and arrive out of order. Make handlers idempotent (a duplicate merge event must not double-award XP) and tolerant of reordering (a PR-closed event arriving before PR-opened). Both are easy to get wrong and produce duplicate reputation.

SECURITY: store the App installation token or PAT in infrastructure only, never in a feature, never in the CLI, never in a URL.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a real PR merged on a real repo completes the corresponding bounty exactly once; a forged webhook signature is rejected; the bounty feature has no GitHub SDK import.

TESTS: integration test with a signed fixture webhook; a duplicate-delivery test asserting idempotency; a reordering test; an architecture test asserting features/ contains no Octokit import.

title: Event ingest (batched) + SSE fan-out, full_state then deltas
description:
Implement the telemetry plane plumbing: batched event ingest and the realtime fan-out, per plan sections 5.1, 7.2, 22, and 25.

THE ARCHITECTURE (section 7.2) - the key backend insight of the whole plan:
  Agents -> Next.js Event Gateway -> {Realtime layer (WS/SSE) -> Browser} + {batched/important -> Neon}
Neon stores DURABLE state only. Realtime is NOT Neon's job.

POST /api/events (section 22): Bearer installation-token -> validate AgentEvent[] (zod, protocol version check) -> resolve session -> persist KEY events -> runtime.emit -> SSE publish.
- Batching: adapters buffer 250ms / up to 50 events. The server REJECTS >100 per batch with 413 plus a Retry-After header.
- Response: { accepted: n, sessionId, resumed: boolean }.

GET /api/events/stream (SSE) (section 22): per-user (web session) or per-battle channel. Sends a full_state snapshot FIRST, then deltas. This exact full_state-then-delta shape is ported from agent-move's Broadcaster (section 1.2 item 4) and the diff-broadcast shape from codemoo/agent-world's stateDiffBroadcast.js (section 28.1 item 12).

MVP CHOICE (section 7.2): SSE, not WebSocket. POST /api/events -> fan-out -> Game UI. SSE is simpler than WS and sufficient for the MVP. Revisit only when measured (section 7.4).

TELEMETRY VERSUS CONTROL (section 5.1): hooks/session-watcher are the telemetry/data plane (passive observation); MCP is the command/control plane (active interaction). NEVER MCP-per-Read/Edit/Bash - that bloats context, costs tokens, drags the workflow, and couples us to per-agent MCP quirks. MCP is NOT event capture.

VOLUME MATH THAT MOTIVATES THE BATCHING (section 7.2): 100 agents x 20 events/s = 2000 DB writes/s, which Neon must NEVER see. This is why the PERSISTED_EVENT_TYPES filter (activity-event-log) and the 250ms/50-event batching are P0 design, not optimization.

DIFF BROADCAST (section 28.1 item 12): port the stateDiffBroadcast + eventsPipeline shape from codemoo/agent-world - broadcast DIFFS, not full state. Also port buildingAssignments.js (repo -> building) and costTracker.js (bounty payout accounting) from the same repo.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a batch over 100 events is rejected with 413 and Retry-After; key events persist while transient events do not; an SSE subscriber receives a full_state snapshot then deltas only; the diff broadcast sends deltas rather than whole-state payloads.

TESTS: integration test for the 413 rejection; a test that transient events never reach the DB; an SSE test asserting the first frame is full_state and subsequent frames are deltas; a load test harness for the 100x20 ev/s scenario (run as a pre-M4 gate per section 17.2, not an M0 gate).

CONSIDERATIONS: the batching parameters (250ms, 50 events, reject over 100 with 413 and Retry-After) are starting values, not constants - they should be configuration, because the right numbers depend on real agent behavior and the 100x20 ev/s load test is what will reveal them. The 413 path matters more than it looks: a client that ignores Retry-After and retries immediately converts a backpressure signal into a self-inflicted stampede. Also, transient events still have to flow to the UI at high rate, so 'we do not persist it' must not quietly become 'we drop it'.

title: HTTP API surface: sessions, bounties, battles, cron
description:
Implement the HTTP route surface listed in plan section 19/22, sitting behind the Public API contract.

ROUTES (section 19 api/ tree, section 22 flows):
- POST /api/events (event-ingest-and-sse bead)
- GET /api/events/stream (SSE)
- POST /api/sessions (HELLO handshake - see contract-session)
- POST /api/sessions/[id]/heartbeat
- POST /api/mcp (MCP Streamable HTTP - built in the P3 MCP bead)
- POST /api/bounties, /api/bounties/[id]/claim, /api/bounties/[id]/submit
- POST /api/battles, /api/battles/[id]
- POST /api/webhooks/github
- POST /api/cron/heartbeat - stale-session sweeper plus season jobs

THE CONTRACT: these routes are CONSUMERS of the application commands/queries defined in contract-public-api.
