They must contain NO game logic - a route handler translates HTTP into an application command and maps the result to a response. This is the same iron rule the CLI follows (section 31) and it is what lets a future Discord bot or GitHub App reuse the commands without reimplementation.

AUTH LAYERING: routes authenticate, then authorize at the application boundary. Bearer installation tokens for agent-facing routes; the human web session for dashboard routes. The two credentials are related but SEPARATE (section 3.4).

THE CRON SWEEWER (section 22): marks sessions stale when (>5 min, no heartbeat, no websocket) as 'disconnected', then 'abandoned' after the grace window. This is what keeps the presence view honest without holding any socket open - and it echoes the plan's decision that heartbeat is a VOLUNTARY agent return cadence, not a held connection (section 13.2).

CONSIDERATIONS: keep handlers thin and push logic down. A route handler that computes a reward is a route handler that will be bypassed by the CLI and produce divergent behavior.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: every route maps 1:1 onto an application command with zero game logic in the handler; the sweeper transitions sessions on schedule; agent routes reject human-session auth and vice versa.

TESTS: route-level integration tests; a parity test asserting HTTP and CLI produce identical application-command effects; an auth-matrix test covering which credential each route accepts.

title: Port HookProvider/TeamProvider seam from pixel-agents
description:
Port the provider seam from pixel-agents into packages/core, per plan section 28.1 item 3 and section 5.3.

SOURCE (MIT, direct copy per section 28.1 item 3):
- pixel-agents/core/src/provider.ts (151 lines) - HookProvider
- pixel-agents/core/src/teamProvider.ts (100 lines) - TeamProvider

WHY A SEAM IN CORE (sections 5.3, 1.1): section 1.1 credits pixel-agents with an explicit agent-agnostic/platform-agnostic roadmap built around a HookProvider seam where 'a new CLI = one subdirectory'. Section 5.3 says core exposes the seam that AgentWatcher implementations plug into. Putting the seam in core (not in an adapter) is what makes the boundary structural rather than conventional, and it is what the dependency-rules bead enforces.

PIXEL-AGENTS REFERENCE ARCHITECTURE (section 1.1): TS monorepo core/server/webview-ui, Fastify+ws, React19+Canvas2D, with an AsyncAPI contract and codegen drift check. Hooks mode posts SessionStart/PreToolUse/PermissionRequest/Stop to /api/hooks/:providerId, with a heuristic fallback scanning ~/.claude/projects/*.jsonl.

ADDITIONAL STEALS FROM THE SAME REPO (section 28.2, learn-only rewrite): agentRuntime.ts, agentStateStore.ts (the SOLE broadcaster - a single choke point for state distribution), fileWatcher.ts / transcriptParser.ts, transport/index.ts branching, and the AsyncAPI-to-Modelina codegen discipline. Section 28.2 says adopt the CONTRACT-FIRST HABIT, not the files - so the AsyncAPI schema-plus-codegen-drift-check practice is worth adopting for our protocol schemas, but the specific generated files are not.

AVOID (section 1.1): VSCode coupling, file-only persistence, Canvas renderer.

ATTRIBUTION: keep the MIT copyright header and add a THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.md entry with the commit SHA (section 28.3).

CONSIDERATIONS: provider identity must be namespaced per providerId so a session is never confused across harnesses; this is the same collision-avoidance problem the identity-resolution logic in feature-agent solves at a higher level.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a new harness can be supported by implementing the seam and adding one subdirectory, with zero core edits; attribution survives; the codegen drift check catches an un-regenerated schema.

TESTS: a contract test suite that every adapter must pass (run it against the _template stub and against each real adapter); a test that providerId namespaces sessions; an architecture test that no adapter imports game code.

title: adapters/_template: the 'new CLI = one subdirectory' promise
description:
Build the adapter template that makes the plan's central onboarding promise true: adding a new coding agent is one subdirectory, not a core change. Per plan sections 1.1, 6, 23, and 27 (M7 DoD).

THE PROMISE (section 1.1, credited to pixel-agents): an explicit agent-agnostic roadmap where 'new CLI = one subdirectory'. Section 27 M7 DoD makes it a testable claim: 'third-party adapter PR merged using only _template + protocol docs; DoD: contributor adds Amp support without touching core.'

FILES (section 23): watcher.ts stub, parser.ts stub, install.ts stub, and a README checklist. Plus index.ts implementing the AgentWatcher interface.

THE INTERFACE every adapter implements (section 23, from agent-move):
  export interface AgentWatcher { start(): Promise<void>; stop(): Promise<void>; }

THE README CHECKLIST must cover: where this harness stores session data, whether it has hooks or requires file/session-log watching, how to normalize its tool names via the shared tool-map, how the installer obtains CONSENT before modifying user config, and how to emit a versioned AgentEvent stream.

CONSENT GATING (section 1.1, from pixel-agents 'consent-gated hook installer'): an adapter that writes into ~/.claude/settings.json or equivalent MUST gate the write behind explicit consent. Section 4 also says 'Never require editing the user's project repo' - so installers touch only global agent config, never the user's code.

WHAT AN ADAPTER MUST NEVER DO (section 23): import game code. Adapters import core + protocol only (enforced by the dependency-rules bead). All adapters emit into the same local buffer feeding POST /api/events via the shared @battle-agents/protocol client.

CONSIDERATIONS: the template is only as good as its checklist. The M7 proof is a third party shipping Amp support from this template alone - so the template must be genuinely self-sufficient, not a stub that assumes tribal knowledge.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a competent developer can add a new harness using only _template + the protocol docs, with zero core edits and zero game-code imports.

TESTS: the template must pass the same adapter contract suite as the real adapters; a CI check that the template is not allowed to import anything outside core/protocol.

title: adapters/claude: hooks primary + JSONL secondary
description:
Implement the Claude Code adapter, per plan sections 6, 23, and 28.2.

PRIMARY PLANE: HOOKS. Claude Code has the richest hook surface of any supported harness (section 6), so the hook plane is primary and session-log reading is secondary. Handler at hooks/hook-handler.ts receives SessionStart, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PermissionRequest, and Stop, normalizes each via normalizeHookEvent(), and emits an AgentEvent.

SECONDARY PLANE: JSONL. parsers/jsonl.ts tails ~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl for fields the hooks do not expose (section 23).

INSTALLER: installer/install-claude.ts writes a hook entry into ~/.claude/settings.json, CONSENT-GATED (pixel-agents pattern), with session-file fallback when hooks are unavailable. Section 6 confirms the fallback shape: AgentMove auto-installs into ~/.claude/settings.json and falls back to session-file watching.

PORT FROM agent-move (section 28.2, learn-only rewrite): watcher/claude parser, the AgentStateManager 30s idle rule, the Broadcaster, TaskGraphManager, full_state-then-delta with exponential-backoff reconnect, and the OpenCode WAL-polling CAUTION that applies to any file-watching path.

UX (section 6, from mcp-coding-agents): 'claude mcp add agent-battle <url>' is the registration shape, proving the npx/MCP-registration UX is feasible.

CONSIDERATIONS: hooks give structured, timely events but only while the agent cooperates; the JSONL tail is the safety net for crashes, forced quits, and missed hooks. Both are needed, and the JSONL reader must not double-count events the hooks already delivered (deduplication is required, not optional).

WHY CLAUDE IS FIRST: it is the reference harness. The normalization logic proven here is what every other adapter reuses.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a live Claude Code session produces a correct, deduplicated AgentEvent stream covering session lifecycle, tools, files, commands, tests, and permission requests; the installer is consent-gated and reversible.

TESTS: fixture-driven tests over real hook payloads; a dedup test proving hook+JSONL do not double-emit; an installer test asserting consent is required and that uninstall restores the original settings.json exactly.

title: adapters/codex: rollout JSONL watcher (no hooks exist)
description:
Implement the Codex adapter, per plan sections 6 and 23.

NO HOOKS EXIST for Codex (section 6) - this adapter is pure session-log watching, which makes it the second reference implementation and the proof that the architecture does not secretly depend on hook support.

MECHANISM (section 23): parsers/rollout.ts watches ~/.codex/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl, polling every 2-3 seconds (the agent-quest precedent, section 28.2).

PORT FROM agent-quest (section 28.2, learn-only rewrite): the providers/ split handling multi-~/.claude* directories plus Codex rollout parsing, and the SessionRegistry / EventBridge concepts. Note agent-quest is MIT but Bun-locked - port the PARSING LOGIC, do not adopt the Bun runtime (section 1.2 item 2 AVOID: 'Bun/Phaser lock-in').

REGISTRATION UX (section 6): 'codex mcp add agent-battle <url>'.

CONSIDERATIONS: polling a file that is being appended to requires care - read incrementally from a tracked offset, tolerate partial/torn lines at the tail, and handle the file appearing or rotating. A naive read-whole-file poll will double-emit or drop events.

SIGNIFICANCE FOR THE ARCHITECTURE: section 22's M1 DoD requires 'two different harnesses visible simultaneously'. This adapter is half of that proof. If a hook-based adapter and a log-watching adapter both work, the telemetry plane is genuinely harness-agnostic.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a live Codex session produces a correct, non-duplicated AgentEvent stream from rollout JSONL alone, running concurrently with a Claude session in the same UI.

TESTS: fixture tests over real rollout JSONL including partial-line and rotation cases; a test that incremental reads do not double-emit; the M1 DoD concurrency test (Claude and Codex both visible at once).

title: adapters/opencode: SQLite session store, careful polling
description:
Implement the OpenCode adapter, per plan sections 1.2 item 4, 6, and 23.

MECHANISM (section 23): parsers/sqlite.ts reads the local SQLite store. Section 6 says 'poll carefully, prefer events'.

THE CAUTION IS EXPLICIT AND REPEATED: section 1.2 item 4 AVOIDs 'high-freq SQLite WAL polling', and section 28.2 repeats 'OpenCode WAL polling CAUTION' as a lesson to carry into our own watcher. Polling a SQLite database in WAL mode at high frequency is a known way to cause lock contention and wasted IO.

IMPLEMENTATION DIRECTION: use BACKOFF polling rather than a hot loop, and prefer event-driven notification where the harness provides it. If we must poll, make the interval adaptive and idle-aware.

PORT FROM agent-move (section 28.2): the watcher/opencode parser approach, while carrying its own OpenCode WAL caution forward rather than inheriting the pattern.

CONSIDERATIONS: SQLite readers must open read-only and must never hold a long-lived write lock on a database the user's editor also owns. A crash of our watcher must not corrupt the user's session data.

WHY IT MATTERS: OpenCode is one of the harnesses that proves the 'cover all coding agents' claim (section 2.2: not a Claude Code plugin). Supporting a non-hook, non-JSONL, database-backed harness broadens the proof considerably.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a live OpenCode session produces a correct AgentEvent stream without contending on the user's database, with adaptive polling rather than a hot loop.

TESTS: fixture tests against a copy of an OpenCode SQLite database; a test that the reader opens read-only; a test that polling backs off when idle; a concurrency test that our reader does not block the harness.

title: adapters/{cursor,pi,gemini}: follow established precedents
description:
Implement the remaining first-party adapters, per plan sections 1.3, 6, and 23.

CURSOR (section 23, Agent Quest precedent): Agent Quest already ships a Cursor adapter (section 1.2 item 2), so follow that precedent. Section 6 adds that Agent Quest covers Cursor and Copilot.

PI (section 23, Agent Intercom precedent): reuse the Agent Intercom protocol shape. Section 1.3 describes Agent Intercom as cross-harness same-machine messaging over one Unix-socket broker with a shared protocol and per-vendor adapters for Pi/Codex/Claude/OpenCode. STEAL the protocol-vendor-per-adapter pattern (section 1.3).

GEMINI CLI (section 6): JSON logs under ~/.gemini.

SECTION 6 GENERAL RULE for the rest: Amp, Grok, and Koda all follow the same AgentWatcher recipe - ONE SUBDIRECTORY EACH (the pixel-agents/agent-move proof). They are intentionally NOT built here; the _template exists precisely so they can be contributed without core changes. Do not gold-plate by pre-building harnesses the template already covers.

Each adapter must: implement AgentWatcher, normalize through the shared tool-map, emit to the same local buffer feeding POST /api/events, and never import game code (section 23).

CONSIDERATIONS: these are lower-traffic harnesses, so the priority is CORRECTNESS of the seam over feature depth. Each must at minimum deliver session lifecycle plus tool events.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: cursor, pi, and gemini each produce a valid AgentEvent stream and pass the shared adapter contract suite; the set collectively demonstrates that adding a harness is routine.

TESTS: the shared adapter contract suite run against each; fixture tests per harness; a coverage check that each emits session lifecycle and tool events at minimum.

title: features/battle: matchmaking, judge, arena (M4 TRIPLE-STAR)
description:
Implement the battle extension - M4, one of the three milestones that prove the idea, per plan sections 10.3, 15.1, 22, 24, and 27.

M4 IS TRIPLE-STAR (section 15.1): same challenge + isolated workspaces + judge + arena/spectator/replay/reward, with modes Speed/Quality/Survival/Boss/Team/Tournament.

COMMANDS (section 24): CreateBattle, JoinBattle, FinishBattle. OWNS: battles and battle_participants tables.

A BATTLE BINDS SESSIONS, NOT AGENTS (section 3.1) - this is a load-bearing invariant and a stated anti-pattern: Battle#918 = Claude/Session#241 vs Codex/Session#552. The WRONG model is 'Battle -> Claude vs Codex' because the same Claude can fight two battles in two sessions. battle_participants references session_ids (section 21).

BATTLE IS NOT FAKE COMBAT (section 2.1): agents must ACTUALLY read/edit/test/build/debug/review. Two real coding agents solve the SAME coding problem in ISOLATED WORKSPACES; the game only visualizes the resulting state. The plan is explicit that this is 'the part no existing repo does completely' and the core differentiator.

MATCH LENGTH (section 10.3, from Clash Royale): 5-15 minutes. Same issue, same tests, isolated repos: code -> test -> debug -> submit.

JUDGING IS SUBSTANCE, NOT SPEED (section 10.3): judge on tests / build / lint / typecheck / diff / security / performance. DEFAULT WEIGHTS stored per battle in battles.weightsJson: {correctness: .5, tests: .2, regression: .1, quality: .1, efficiency: .1}. Ties: faster valid submission wins (Speed) or shared win (Tournament).

THE WEIGHTS MUST BE PUBLIC (section 17.4): judge weights are published per match. This is both a fairness property and a trust property - a hidden rubric is indistinguishable from a rigged one.

CODING BEHAVIOR MAPS TO STATS, NEVER TOKENS TO DAMAGE (sections 2.2, 10.3): Edit + tests pass -> +XP; Edit + fail -> small XP; 5 consecutive failures -> damage; fixing your own bug -> critical hit. Stats: STR (successful changes) / INT (reasoning) / WIS (tool selection) / LUK (unexpected recovery), with DEF (tests) and DEX (fast iterations). Section 2.2 explicitly BANS 'token-count-as-damage'.

BATTLE STATES (section 3.2): RUNNING / PAUSED / COMPLETED / ABANDONED / EXPIRED. Disconnect during a battle -> grace period -> reconnect? resume : abandoned.

DECLARED CAPABILITY DEPENDENCY (section 24): requires: ['reputation.read'], degrading to open battles when reputation is uninstalled. This is the removal-test proof - it is a real architectural demonstration, not decoration.

ANTI-CHEAT IS TBD (section 17.4): fairness is in scope for M4 (public weights, mandatory isolated workspaces); full anti-cheat is explicitly still open. Do not let this bead expand into anti-cheat engineering.

SUCCESS CRITERIA (section 27 M4 DoD): 1v1 battle on the same issue, isolated workspaces, public weights, judge run, replay URL shareable, XP/rep applied - and the DoD test is that a LOGGED-OUT user can open the share link and see the full timeline.

TESTS: judge unit tests per criterion with fixtures; an isolation test proving one participant cannot see or affect the other's workspace; a tie-handling test; the logged-out replay-share DoD test; a removal test asserting battles degrade gracefully without reputation.

CONSIDERATIONS: the honest risk is that a battle is only as interesting as the honesty of its judging. Everything here - public weights, mandatory isolation, deterministic judge - exists so the result is defensible. A judge whose weights are hidden, or a workspace leak between participants, destroys the feature faster than any amount of visual polish can build it. Related: battles are expensive (two agents, isolated environments, test runs), so the token and compute cost per battle is a real product constraint that belongs in this design, not deferred to operations. Anti-cheat is explicitly still open (section 17.4) - document the gap rather than implying it is solved.

title: Isolated workspace provisioner + judge pipeline + hook gates
description:
Build the mechanical substrate under feature-battle: isolated workspaces, the judge run pipeline, and pre-flight gates. Per plan sections 10.3, 17.4, 22, and 28.1 items 4-5.

ISOLATED WORKSPACES ARE MANDATORY (section 17.4), not optional. Each participant works in its own sandboxed copy so neither can read nor corrupt the other's work. The battle is meaningless without this.

THE JUDGE RUN (section 22), per participant workspace: install -> typecheck -> lint -> test suite -> regression (base-branch test set) -> diff stats -> security grep rules. Then the weighted score from battles.weightsJson. Judge output IS the replay seed (section 22) - so the judge must emit an ordered, structured, attributable event stream, not just a number.

HOOK GATES AS PRE-CHECKS (section 28.1 item 4, direct copy from agent-dashboard, MIT): port adapters/claude-code/hooks/ scripts - commit-lint, test-gate, destructive-warn, block-main-commit - into battle judge pre-checks and features/battle workspace guards. Also port the skills/{feature,fix,pr}/SKILL.md FRONTMATTER SHAPE as our extension/skill contract model (section 1.1 credits agent-dashboard with this).

WHY GATES MATTER: a 'destructive-warn' or 'block-main-commit' gate is precisely the kind of guard that makes it safe to let autonomous agents work in parallel sandboxes. They are cheap insurance and the plan explicitly wants them.

SECURITY GREP RULES belong in the judge (section 22) - keep them as DATA (a rules table), not hardcoded branches, so rules can be updated without a deploy of the battle engine.

CONSIDERATIONS: judge runs are the slowest and most failure-prone part of a battle. A participant whose workspace fails to install should lose or forfeit by a stated rule, not hang the match. Decide and document timeout/forfeit semantics; a battle that cannot terminate is worse than no battle.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: two participants are provably isolated; the judge produces a weighted, explained score; the gate scripts block the specified dangerous operations and pass through the safe ones.

TESTS: isolation test (cross-workspace access attempts fail); judge fixture tests per criterion; gate tests proving destructive-warn blocks and commit-lint passes; a timeout/forfeit test.

title: Battle replay builder + shareable replay URL
description:
Build the battle replay - the plan's most viral feature, per plan sections 2.3, 15.1, 22, and 8.

WHY REPLAY IS THE VIRAL HOOK (section 2.3): the plan judges Battle Replay to be EVEN MORE viral than the Claude-vs-Codex demo. It is the social mechanism: timestamped event log -> battle -> result -> URL. It is also the mechanism by which replays attract sponsors, and sponsors attract more agents (section 2.4 network effect). The example timeline the plan sketches: 00:01 accept quest / 00:08 starts research / 00:17 edits auth.ts / 00:23 discovers vulnerability / 00:41 test fails / 00:48 patches bug / 01:12 critical hit / 01:20 tests 47/47 / 01:20 winner.

DATA: battles.replayJson holds the event timeline; battles.winnerSessionId holds the result. Replay is BUILT FROM THE ACTIVITY LOG (section 30) plus the judge output (section 22, 'judge output IS the replay seed') - not assembled separately.

VIEW (section 22): apps/web/app/(app)/replay/[replayId]/page.tsx renders the event timeline, PixiJS arena playback, and share metadata including an og:image generated from the final frame.

THE DoD THAT MATTERS (section 27 M4): share the replay link with a LOGGED-OUT user and they see the full timeline. This forces a real design decision - the public replay must be viewable without a session, which means the replay data is public even though the account is not. Decide what participant detail (agent names, repo names) is safe to expose publicly; this is a privacy consideration the plan does not spell out, so resolve it deliberately.

ALSO: diff-streaming over the websocket for arena efficiency (section 8), using the codemoo stateDiffBroadcast pattern (section 28.1 item 12).

CONSIDERATIONS: replay URLs are the viral vector, so they must be stable, guess-resistant, and cheap to serve. Consider whether replays should expire or be pruned (an activity-log retention question, cross-referenced with activity-event-log).

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a completed battle produces a replay URL; a logged-out visitor sees the complete timeline; the og:image renders.

TESTS: the logged-out DoD test; a determinism test (same event stream yields the same replay); a test that replay construction reads from event_log rather than feature tables.

title: features/guild: teams, treasury, guild quests (M6)
description:
Implement the guild feature per plan sections 10.4, 11.3, and 24. M6 scope.

SCOPE (section 24): teams, treasury, guild quests.

GUILD AS THE SOCIAL ENDGAME (section 10.4): shared agents, projects, and research. Guild quests such as 'fix 10 issues in project X' where each agent contributes. Weekly Guild A vs Guild B tallies. Explicitly NO pay-to-win (section 10.4).

GUILD TREASURY (section 11.3): guilds fund bounties collectively, connecting to the open-funding model.

TFT TEAM COMPOSITION (section 10.2): team TRAITS and SYNERGY, not raw stacking. Roles are Researcher / Coder / Tester / Reviewer; a Coder+Tester+Reviewer combination yields a validation bonus. CRITICAL: role comes from player BEHAVIOR, not from the model - '3 Claude' should NOT just be 3 Claude; it can be a Debugger, a Researcher, and a Security specialist. This directly reuses the build-derivation from feature-progression.

CLEANEST EXAMPLE IN THE PLAN (section 2.4): 'Quang's Claude Lv37 Architect with Refactor special' is a CHALLENGEABLE SOCIAL IDENTITY, not a model name. Agent = AI + developer configuration (prompts, tools, memory). That identity layer is what pixel-agent projects lack and it is the network-effect foundation.

ACL PATTERN (section 1.1, from Agentainer's can_talk_to): use a declared ACL concept for guild messaging rather than letting any agent DM any agent. This also sets up the messaging.md etiquette doc (section 26).

M6 DoD (section 27): two users' agents in one guild complete a team bounty.

CONSIDERATIONS: guild state is strongly social and therefore strongly abuse-prone (alt accounts, collusion, guild-shopping for favorable bounties). Section 17 does not cover social abuse in detail - note it as an open risk rather than pretending it is solved.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: two users' agents join one guild and complete a team bounty; role synergies are computed from behavior; messaging respects the ACL.

TESTS: the M6 DoD integration test; a synergy-calculation test; an ACL enforcement test; a removal test that guild uninstalls cleanly.

title: features/social: messaging, profiles, leaderboard
description:
Implement the social feature per plan sections 1.3, 8, 13, and 24. M6 scope.

SCOPE (section 24): messages, profiles, leaderboard queries.

SCHEMA (section 21): messages: id, fromAgentId -> agents, toAgentId -> agents, guildId, body, createdAt. Note the nullable toAgentId plus guildId - messages are either agent-to-agent DMs or guild broadcasts.

PORT THE MESSAGING SHAPE FROM cross-agent-teams-mcp (section 28.1 item 8, MIT): register-agent / send / broadcast / poke / inbox / bind-runtime-identity tool shapes, refactored into inbox + outbox plus poke/wake fanout over Neon and SSE. Section 1.3 credits this repo with the identity-registry + inbox/outbox + poke/wake fanout pattern and specifically the identity-vs-session split - which is already locked in contract-agent-identity.

WIRE-LEVEL PRECEDENTS (section 1.1 section C): karansag/agent-swarm is a delivery layer UNDER orchestrators - it holds agent registration, stable session ID, model, tmux pane, message history, and delivery status, and injects messages directly into the agent's terminal pane. That last capability (injecting into a live agent's context) is the genuinely interesting one for us and should be evaluated, not dismissed.

PUBLIC AGENT PROFILE (section 2.4): level, battle history, W/L, achievements, projects, guild. This is the network-effect artifact - profiles attract challenges, challenges produce replays, replays attract sponsors.

LEADERBOARD (section 2.3, 15.1): part of the tournament content engine.

SCOPE DISCIPLINE (section 17.8): social is M6, NOT MVP. No marketplace, no trading, no guild war, no housing, no crafting in this phase.

CONSIDERATIONS: agent-to-agent messaging is a prompt-injection surface. An agent receiving a DM from another agent is reading untrusted text authored by (or on behalf of) someone else. Design the trust boundary deliberately - this is a real security consideration the plan does not address, so surface it rather than shipping it blind.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: agents exchange messages via the protocol and CLI; public profiles render battle history; leaderboards query correctly.

TESTS: messaging round-trip test; an ACL/authorization test on who may DM whom; a test that public profile data excludes private fields; a removal test.

title: game-client: PixiJS v8 world mirroring age-of-agents
description:
Build the PixiJS game client by mirroring the age-of-agents client skeleton, per plan sections 8, 25, and 28.1 item 6.

DIRECT COPY (section 28.1 item 6, MIT): mirror .tmp/age-of-agents/packages/client/src/game/ FILE FOR FILE - view.ts, unit.ts, tilemap.ts, projection.ts, pathfind.ts, autotile.ts, building-sprites.ts, camera-guards.ts - plus the dual public/assets/{fantasy,scifi}/ packs (buildings, decorations, heroes, tilemap) as placeholder themes. Section 1.2 item 1 calls this the BEST PixiJS v8 reference and says 'STEAL nearly all client structure'. age-of-agents is MIT, so its code AND its shipped assets are covered - keep its LICENSE header and add a NOTICE entry.

WHY MIRROR RATHER THAN DESIGN (section 1.2 item 1): the reference already proves pixi-viewport + React19 + zustand, a clean view/unit/tilemap/tilemap-iso/projection/pathfind/autotile/building-sprites/camera-guards decomposition, and a dual fantasy/scifi asset pack structure. Re-deriving that decomposition from scratch is wasted effort.

EXPERIENCE TARGET (section 1.2 item 1): the reference uses pixi-viewport with React19 and zustand. Adopt that stack shape.

THEN EXTEND (section 25):
- zones.ts - config-driven {tool|event -> zone} mapping, adding bounty-board, battle-arena, guild-hall to the AgentMove zone set
- net/client.ts - SSE client: full_state to hydrate the store, then deltas to patch
- state/store.ts - zustand or event-emitter store
- scenes/ - city.ts, arena.ts, guild-hall.ts
- sprites/sprite-factory.ts - programmatic 16x16@3x PLACEHOLDER sprites (agent-move pattern) until the asset shortlist lands; this keeps V0 unblocked by art

PERFORMANCE (section 25): diff updates only (the codemoo lesson), delta-capped rAF loop (pixel-agents gameLoop.ts pattern), sprite cache.

SCOPE (section 17.8): the game client is NOT in the M0-M4 MVP. M2 ships 'with zero game UI' precisely so real utility lands before art. This is the gimmick-risk defense (section 17.1).

SUCCESS CRITERIA: the world renders and is driven ONLY by normalized events; zone mapping is config-driven; performance holds the diff/rAF/caching discipline.

TESTS: a render smoke test; a test that the client derives all state from the event stream with no hardcoded agent names; a performance smoke test on the delta path; an architecture test that presentation imports features but never the reverse.

CONSIDERATIONS: mirroring age-of-agents file-for-file is right up to a point - the temptation is to keep mirroring as our needs diverge (we add bounty/battle/guild zones; they do not), and past that point the copy becomes a straitjacket. Name that boundary explicitly: mirror the view/unit/tilemap decomposition, then own the divergence. Second, the programmatic sprite factory is what keeps V0 unblocked by art, so resist deleting it once real assets land - it is also what makes the client testable without an asset pipeline.

title: Next.js UI: dashboard, bounty board, arena, replay, agent cards
description:
Build the web UI surface per plan section 8.

MAIN SCREEN OPTIONS (section 8). The plan offers a pixel-city main screen and a BOUNTY BOARD AS FIRST SCREEN OPTION - and the bounty board is better aligned with the M2-is-valuable-without-game-UI strategy. The board: HOT BOUNTIES list ($2000 SSO, $750 memleak, $250 OAuth, $50 CLI bug with competitor counts) -> bounty detail (repo, issue, reward, requirements, [ENTER BATTLE], competitors).

DASHBOARD (section 8, from the conversation): top bar (Agent Battle, notifications, coins, level) / CODING CITY map (Guild Hall, Research Lab, character, Arena, Workshop, Quest Board) / bottom tabs (QUESTS, AGENTS, GUILD, ARENA, PROFILE).

AGENT CARD (section 3.2 + section 10.1): level, current quest and session, skill bars, [Enter Arena] [View History] [Join Guild]. The dashboard agent list must show online AND offline agents with Level/XP and 'Last seen 12m ago' - a dead session must never make a character vanish.

REPLAY VIEW: see battle-replay.

GUILD HALL with a map editor inside the client (section 8, agent-quest editor precedent).

DIFF STREAMING over the websocket in the arena for efficiency (section 8).

PRODUCT SHAPE (section 11.4): BOUNTY MARKET (issues, sponsors, rewards) + GAME WORLD (agents, guilds, projects) + ARENA (PvP, battles, tournaments) over AGENT RUNTIME (MCP/hooks/GitHub).

CONSIDERATIONS: the plan is emphatic that the web is a VIEW, not the game - every loop must be playable via the protocol alone (section 34). The UI must not become the only path to any action, or the machine-native rule is broken.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: bounty board, agent cards, and replay render from real data; offline agents display correctly; no loop is web-only.

TESTS: component/integration tests; a snapshot for the agent card's online/offline states; the E2E smoke covering login -> connect -> claim -> replay render (section 40).

STATE WARNING, added 2026-09-24: `apps/web` currently exists as a plain TypeScript library named `@battle-agents/web`. It is NOT a web app: no `next` dependency, no `next.config.mjs`, no `app/` directory, and its build is `tsc`. This placeholder came from the scaffold step, where it was an incorrect instruction, and the mistake is the misleading name rather than any broken code.

Consequences for whoever picks this up:
- Do NOT import `next/...` into it yet. Next.js is not installed, so such an import will not resolve.
- `docker compose up` (the M0 local-dev DoD) cannot serve a real app until Next.js lands, because there is no server to serve.
- This bead owns the fix: add `next`, `react`, `react-dom`, a `next.config.mjs`, a minimal `app/layout.tsx`, and an `app/api/health/route.ts`. Keep that minimal and infrastructure-only. Actual VISUAL work stays blocked until DESIGN.md exists, because antislop R-37 forbids building UI without design direction. A framework shell plus a health endpoint is not visual design and is not blocked.

title: Animation core spike: minimal skeletal runtime subset
description:
Spike a MINIMAL skeletal animation runtime, informed by learn-spine, per plan sections 9.1-9.5 and 25.

THE LESSON (section 9.3): learn-spine is NOT a Spine tutorial. It is a feasibility prototype of an AGENT-OPERATED 2D animation web platform. Architecture: Agent -> WebMCP -> Command Layer -> Project Session -> Animation Core -> Pose -> PixiJS -> WebGL. React is UI only; the core has NO DOM/React/WebMCP dependencies; editor and player SHARE the core so they can never render divergently.

ADOPT from learn-spine (section 9.4): the core/pose/renderer split; STABLE IDs (bones identified by stable id, never by name - names change, ids do not); revisioned commands carrying expectedRevision + requestId so concurrent edits CONFLICT instead of silently overwriting; the observe-modify-render loop (modify -> render -> observe -> diagnose -> modify again); shared editor/player core.

AVOID (section 9.4): cloning the architecture wholesale; treating it as a production renderer; building a FULL ANIMATION EDITOR. We need a minimal RUNTIME subset, not an editor product. A character needs idle/walk/attack/take-damage/victory, not a keyframe timeline UI.

PIPELINE TO REPLICATE (section 9.3): FK -> IK -> Mesh skinning -> Region transform -> Renderer, driven by evaluate(Project, PoseRequest). The renderer NEVER solves IK - it receives computed geometry. This separation is the whole point.

WHY SKELETAL AND NOT SPRITESHEETS (section 9.2): spritesheets hardcode animation; skeletal lets an agent manipulate STRUCTURED STATE (moveAgent, attack, takeDamage, equip, changeSkin, playAnimation, setPose) with the game engine deciding the animation. Agent state (reading, testing, failed, fixed, battling) selects reading/terminal/damage/victory/attack animations.

STATUS CAVEATS (section 9.3): the reference author reports perf Gate 1 FAIL at the measurement point, physics untested, production-readiness unproven, and MVP output deferred. Treat it as a RESEARCH PROTOTYPE, not a Spine replacement, and do not benchmark against it as a quality bar.

NO PREMATURE OPTIMIZATION (section 9.3): the reference deliberately avoided WebGPU/WASM/Web Workers until a bottleneck was MEASURED. Do the same - measure first.

INTEGRATION (section 25): the animation feature is a CONSUMER - GameState -> AnimationState -> Pose frames for the game client - with ZERO game logic. Removing it must leave the game fully playable.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a character renders from skeleton data and animates through the agent-state mappings; the core has no React/DOM/WebMCP imports; it is removable.

TESTS: golden-frame tests for pose evaluation; a determinism test (same Project + PoseRequest -> same pose); a test that the core module graph excludes React/DOM/WebMCP; a removal test.

CONSIDERATIONS: the scope trap is building an editor. The learn-spine reference includes a full editor with undo/redo, checkpoints, and observation tooling, and it is genuinely impressive - but we need a runtime subset that plays a handful of animations, not an authoring product. Building the editor is a multi-month diversion that serves no milestone. Second: because the reference reports its own perf gate failing, do not treat it as a quality bar or copy its rendering approach uncritically; measure our own bottleneck before optimizing, which is the same discipline the reference itself followed by not prematurely reaching for WebGPU/WASM/Workers.

title: Curated CC0/consistent asset shortlist + license tracking
description:
Curate the game asset shortlist and enforce per-pack license tracking, per plan sections 14 and 28.3.

SOURCES (section 14): OpenGameArt (fast prototyping - characters, tilesets, RPG maps, UI, SFX); itch.io (largest - pixel character/RPG, cyberpunk/arena tilesets, UI, battle VFX); Kenney (clean consistent packs - characters, UI, icons, buildings, particles); CraftPix and GameDevMarket (commercial production art); GitHub (CC0 packs - VERIFY each license, never assume).

THE DELIVERABLE (section 14): a curated shortlist of roughly 10-20 packs, free/CC0, in a SINGLE consistent style. The plan explicitly offered this as a follow-up and section 18 build-order item 9 includes it. Do it BEFORE commissioning art.

ART DIRECTION (section 14): cyberpunk / developer-workstation / RPG-arena. Tentative skins: Claude -> Mage, Codex -> Knight, Gemini -> Alchemist, OpenCode -> Rogue, Pi -> Hacker. CRITICAL CONSTRAINT: skins ONLY - never hardcode class to model. Class is behavior-derived (see feature-progression); the skin is cosmetic and must be swappable. An agent may also carry its own custom loadout.

LICENCE HYGIENE (sections 14, 17.7, 28.3): the code is MIT, but EACH ASSET PACK KEEPS ITS OWN LICENSE, stored beside the pack at public/assets/<pack>/LICENSE.txt. The shortlist MUST record per-pack license BEFORE merge. Never assume a GitHub repo's assets are freely usable.

IMMEDIATE UNBLOCKER (section 28.1 item 1): the CC0 tiny-swords pack from agent-quest is vendored unchanged for V0 - sprites plus its LICENSE.txt - giving instant characters and tiles before the shortlist lands. That copy is already sanctioned; this bead is about the longer-term curated set.

SCOPE DISCIPLINE (section 17.7): decide the game-asset license separately from the code MIT license, and track per-pack licenses. This is a real decision, not a formality - mixing a GPL art pack into an MIT repo would contaminate it.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a shortlist of 10-20 same-style packs with recorded per-pack licenses exists; every merged pack ships its LICENSE.txt; no pack is merged without a verified license.

TESTS: a CI check that every directory under public/assets/ has a LICENSE.txt; a check that the recorded license in the shortlist matches the shipped file.

CONSIDERATIONS: style consistency is the actual selection criterion, not license or price - a perfect set of individually excellent packs in five different visual styles is worse than a smaller set that looks like one game, because visual incoherence reads as 'amateur project' instantly. Second: the license check is per-pack and must be re-verified at merge time, not at selection time; licenses change and packs get relicensed. Third: the plan is explicit that art licenses are tracked SEPARATELY from the MIT code license, so resist the convenience of assuming everything in the repo is MIT because the code is.

title: MCP adapter: 5 stable primitives over the capability registry
description:
Implement the MCP Streamable HTTP adapter, per plan sections 5.1, 22, 26, 32, 33, and 36.

CRITICAL SCOPE CORRECTION (sections 31, 32, 33): MCP is NOT P0. Protocol/API + CLI ship first; MCP is an adapter on the SAME protocol later. Section 33's P3 list puts 'MCP adapter' explicitly in phase 3, and section 36 makes interfaces/{cli,mcp,api,websocket} EQUAL capability consumers rather than MCP-first.

THE SURFACE IS EXACTLY 5 PRIMITIVES (section 32): discover, search, inspect, act, observe. NOT the old domain-operation tool list.

BANNED IMPLEMENTATION (sections 5.1, 32, 33): the section 1.3-era tool list - register_agent, get_world, get_quests, get_opponents, challenge_agent, accept_battle, send_message, inspect_enemy, claim_reward, spawn_agent, quest/party/progress/report/move and so on - describes CAPABILITIES IN THE REGISTRY and must NEVER be implemented verbatim as MCP tools. That verbatim list IS the tool-explosion path section 32 bans. Adding Guild must change the registry, not the tool surface.

WHY THE PRIMITIVES EXIST (section 32): N features x M operations collapses to 100-200 MCP tools, which is undiscoverable and bloats agent context. 'Cover every capability, expose few stable primitives.' discover() is LAZY - top-level domains first, per-domain detail on demand, NEVER the full 200-capability firehose at connect time.

ANTI-GOD-TOOL GUARD: act() dispatches TYPED registry-defined actions (defineAction), never act({action: string, payload: any}). A bogus action id must be a compile error.

MCP IS THE CONTROL PLANE, NOT EVENT CAPTURE (section 5.1, section 5 'MCP khong nen dung de capture moi event'): NEVER make the agent call MCP after every Read/Edit/Bash. That bloats context, costs tokens, drags the workflow, and couples us to per-agent MCP quirks. Hooks/session-watcher carry telemetry; MCP carries commands.

AUTH (sections 3.4, 22, 4): short-lived installation token from the section 4 flow, obtained via MCP OAuth. NEVER put a raw token in the MCP URL (?token= leaks into logs and history) - the plan's own bad example.

ONBOARDING UX this enables (section 4, from mcp-coding-agents): 'claude mcp add agent-battle https://agentbattle.gg/mcp' then browser auth, then a terminal confirmation showing Agent, Account, and Project. This is the proof that 'login -> add MCP -> authorize -> play' needs no separate CLI install.

REVIEW GUARD (section 36): any PR adding interfaces/mcp/* implementation code FOR A SPECIFIC GAME FEATURE (instead of registry entries) fails review.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: an agent connects over MCP, discovers domains lazily, performs a full bounty loop via the 5 primitives, and the tool count stays at 5 no matter how many features are installed.

TESTS: a tool-count test asserting exactly 5 primitives regardless of installed features; a lazy-discovery test; a protocol-loop integration test; an architecture test that no per-feature MCP tool modules exist.

CONSIDERATIONS: the pull toward a richer tool surface is strongest right after a real agent struggles with the 5 primitives - and that is precisely the moment the plan's argument applies. If discover is too coarse, the fix is finer-grained REGISTRY metadata, not a sixth tool. A useful forcing function: any proposed sixth primitive must demonstrate a capability that genuinely cannot be expressed as discover/search/inspect/act/observe. Related, keep MCP clearly on the control plane - it is tempting to use it for notifications or telemetry because it is already connected, and that is the exact conflation section 5.1 warns against.

title: Publish skill.md + heartbeat.md + messaging.md + events.md
description:
Publish the agent-facing protocol documentation, per plan sections 13, 26, and 33.

MIRROR MOLTBOOK'S SHAPE (sections 13.1, 28.1 item 11): adapt the moltbook skill.md / heartbeat.md / messaging.md / skill.json structure (MIT) to our own protocol docs in apps/web/public/. Publish skill.md, heartbeat.md, messaging.md, events.md, plus skill.json with a version pin.

VERIFY BEFORE COPYING (section 29 - IMPORTANT CORRECTION): the plan's architecture review found that skill.md could NOT be fetched directly (the server returns Markdown content-type the tooling could not parse), so NO Moltbook implementation details asserted from that file are trustworthy. Everywhere the plan describes Moltbook mechanics (api_key flow, ~4h heartbeat, claim flow, rate limits), treat it as UNVERIFIED HYPOTHESIS, not fact. Read moltbook's SOURCE or API docs directly to confirm; never infer from a skill.md summary.

WHAT SURVIVES regardless (section 29): the architectural distinction is independently sound - Human GitHub Account -> Agent Identity (credentials, progression, reputation, history) -> Sessions (ephemeral). Keep the principle, drop the citation certainty. See the moltbook-verification bead.

THE DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS (section 33): instructions are NOT transport, NOT protocol, NOT runtime. skill.md is PROMPT INPUT, not an executable plugin - which is exactly why it is cross-framework and why ANY skills-capable agent can participate without a per-harness adapter.

TWO EXTENSION LAYERS (section 13.1): PLATFORM extensions (our Bounty/Battle/Guild/Trading/Tournament modules) versus AGENT extensions (the agent's own installed skills - a battle skill, a github skill, and so on). The platform exposes the protocol; the agent composes skills. Conflating these is the mistake to avoid.

THE DOC (section 26, adapted): API base URL; Bearer agent_token auth, register once and the same key equals the same character; capabilities (register identity, inspect character, discover quests and bounties, claim bounty, join and fight battles, submit a result via PR URL, message agents, receive events); the heartbeat loop (check quests, battle invitations, guild messages, bounty updates, then act and report); and the rules (sessions are ephemeral and may close any time while the character persists; XP comes from merged PRs and passing tests, NEVER token counts; battle scoring weights are public per match).

HEARTBEAT SEMANTIC (section 13.2): a VOLUNTARY agent return cadence on a timer - NOT a held-open socket. Ours checks quests, battle invites, guild messages, and bounty updates. This is a deliberate architectural choice: it means an agent can close its terminal for days and its character persists.

VERSION CHECK (section 26): check the version on every handshake; on mismatch, warn and link the changelog.

CONSIDERATIONS: these docs are the onboarding surface for third-party agents, so clarity is the product. An agent that misreads 'XP comes from tokens' will game the economy.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: all four docs plus skill.json are published; a skills-capable agent can participate using ONLY these docs and no per-harness adapter; the version pin is enforced at handshake.

TESTS: a docs-completeness check (all four files present, skill.json version matches PROTOCOL_VERSION); a version-mismatch handshake test; a lint pass asserting no doc contradicts a locked decision (e.g. no token-as-XP claim).

title: External extension packages + public protocol/SDK (M7)
description:
Open the ecosystem per plan sections 16 and 33 (M7).

WHAT M7 IS (section 15.1): open ecosystem via MIT protocol/SDK covering adapters, agents, clients, and arenas - the contributor flywheel.

LICENSE POSTURE (sections 16, 35): MIT everywhere, whole repo, public from day one. Rationale: a fun-game OSS flywheel maximizes stars, forks, and contributions; MIT is simpler than Apache-2.0 and avoids copyleft fear; it is commercial-use safe. THE MOAT IS COMMUNITY + AGENTS + BOUNTIES + HISTORY + REPUTATION + GUILDS, NOT SOURCE. Precedents cited: Kubernetes, Kafka, Spark, TensorFlow, Android - forks cannot fork ecosystems; LiveKit - open core to hosted cloud value. Custom 'MIT + no-compete' licenses were REJECTED (they are not OSS). Trademark, brand, and domain are protected separately, since MIT/Apache grant no trademark rights beyond attribution.

FORKS ARE WELCOMED (section 16): forks like 'Agent Arena' or 'Coding Wars' are welcome IF protocol-compatible - and that compatibility is precisely what would make us the standard.

THE FLYWHEEL NEEDS MORE THAN A LICENSE (section 16): docs, easy dev, clear architecture, good-first-issues, fun visible results (adapter, reporter, or battle-mode PRs), a useful protocol, and active maintainers. A permissive license alone does not produce contributors. This bead is where that non-license work happens.

BANNED (section 29.2): a plugin MARKETPLACE, a plugin INSTALLER, dynamic/remote plugin loading, distributed event infrastructure, and microservices. The extension model is EXPLICIT COMPOSITION via createRuntime({extensions: [...]}), not a dynamic loader. Do not build an installer here.

PACKAGE SHAPE (section 33): features/extensions declare capabilities and know NOTHING about MCP/CLI/REST/Web. External packages install the same way internal ones do - as GameFeature objects. A third-party world or battle mode is just another extension.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: an external package can be published and consumed as a GameFeature without patching core; the protocol/SDK is documented well enough to write a client from scratch.

TESTS: a test that an out-of-tree extension installs and uninstalls through the public API only; a removal test for the external extension.

CONSIDERATIONS: the plan's moat argument is worth restating as an engineering constraint rather than a slogan - the defensibility is community, agents, bounties, history, reputation, and guilds, NOT source code. That has a practical consequence: breaking protocol compatibility is expensive, so versioning and compatibility guarantees deserve more care here than typical feature work. Second, resist building the ecosystem tooling early. Section 29.2 bans a plugin marketplace, a plugin installer, and dynamic loading; explicit composition is the model. Publishing packages and documenting the protocol is enough until real third parties force otherwise.

title: Contributor onboarding: docs, AGENTS.md, good-first-issues
description:
Build the contributor experience, per plan section 16.

WHY THIS IS A SEPARATE BEAD: section 16 argues the flywheel needs MORE than a permissive license - it needs docs, easy dev, clear architecture, good-first-issues, fun visible results, a useful protocol, and active maintainers. The MIT decision (section 35) is necessary but NOT sufficient. Skipping this is the most likely way the project has a license and no contributors.

DELIVERABLES:
- AGENTS.md describing the project for coding agents (WHAT/WHY/HOW, progressive disclosure)
- README that states the vision, the MIT license, and the architecture at a glance
- Architecture documentation explaining the four contracts (section 29.1) and WHY they were locked first - a contributor who does not understand the extension boundary will break it
- A local dev guide pointing at 'git clone, cp .env.example .env, docker compose up' (section 37) - the low-friction entry is a real contributor-acquisition feature
- Good-first-issues, ideally of the FUN-VISIBLE kind the plan calls for: adapter PRs, reporter PRs, battle-mode PRs. These let a newcomer ship something that shows up on screen rather than fixing an internal chore
- Documented failure modes for the local OAuth path (section 39): redirect_uri_mismatch, missing Better Auth secret, DB unreachable - the three things that will actually block a newcomer's first run

ARCHITECTURE COMMUNICATION: the removal test and the dependency rules are only meaningful if contributors understand the intent. Explain that adding a feature must never edit core/cli/mcp implementations (section 33) and that this is checked in review.

CONSIDERATIONS: contributor friction is highest at first-run. Measure it: have someone unfamiliar run the local setup and log every point of confusion.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a newcomer goes from clone to running app plus a merged first PR without undocumented help; the docs state MIT and only MIT (section 35: any Apache-2.0 mention is stale).

TESTS: a docs-link checker; a CI job that runs the documented local-setup steps verbatim so the guide cannot rot; a grep asserting no stale Apache-2.0 claim in docs.

title: M7 proof: third-party adapter merged with zero core edits
description:
Prove the extensibility architecture is real, per plan section 27 (M7 DoD) and section 6.

THE DoD, VERBATIM (section 27): 'third-party adapter PR merged using only _template + protocol docs; DoD: contributor adds Amp support without touching core.'

WHY THIS IS A BEAD RATHER THAN A MILESTONE LABEL: the plan's central architectural claim is 'add feature = add module + register capability, zero core edits' (section 12.1) and 'new CLI = one subdirectory' (section 1.1). A claim like that is only worth something if it survives contact with a real contributor who was not in the room when it was designed. This bead is the falsification test for the architecture.

PROCEDURE:
1. Have someone (or an agent working only from the written docs) implement the Amp adapter using adapters/_template plus the protocol docs - not by reading our feature code
2. Merge it through the normal review path
3. Verify the diff touches ZERO files under core/, interfaces/, and other features

ARCHITECTURE-FAILURE SIGNAL (sections 33, 36): if adding Amp requires ANY edit to core/, cli/, or mcp/ implementations, that is an architecture FAILURE and the correct response is to fix the architecture - not to relax the rule.

SUPPORTING LEGS from the research: section 1.1 credits pixel-agents with an agent-agnostic roadmap where a new CLI is one subdirectory; section 6 says Amp, Grok, and Koda all follow the same AgentWatcher recipe; section 26's skill.md exists so that ANY skills-capable agent can participate without a per-harness adapter at all.

WHAT TO LEARN FROM A FAILURE: if the template proves insufficient, the gap is real product debt in the template and protocol docs - fix those, do not special-case Amp.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: the Amp adapter is merged with a diff limited to packages/adapters/amp/ plus a manifest entry.

TESTS: a CI assertion that the Amp adapter diff introduced no changes outside its own directory; the adapter contract suite passes for Amp.

CONSIDERATIONS: the temptation, when this fails, is to special-case the new harness - add a field to the provider interface, a conditional in the registry, a branch in an adapter. That converts a false claim about the architecture into a true but much weaker one, and it is how a 'pluggable' system becomes a switchboard. The correct response to a failure is to fix the template or the protocol docs, then re-run. Also worth resisting: letting the proof be performed by someone who already knows the codebase, since insider knowledge is exactly the variable that would mask the gap.

title: Verify Moltbook claims from source (section 29 correctness pass)
description:
Resolve the unverified Moltbook claims flagged in plan section 29, by reading source or API docs directly.

THE PROBLEM (section 29): the architecture review found that skill.md could NOT be fetched directly (the server returns Markdown content-type the tooling could not parse), so NO Moltbook implementation details asserted from that file are TRUSTWORTHY. Every place the plan describes Moltbook mechanics - api_key flow, ~4h heartbeat, claim flow, rate limits, human-escalation policy - is UNVERIFIED HYPOTHESIS, not fact.

THE RULE (section 29): keep the PRINCIPLE, drop the citation certainty. Never infer implementation details from a skill.md summary. Read the source or the API docs directly.

WHAT MUST BE CHECKED against .tmp/moltbook (a small 7-file MIT skill-spec repo, already cloned): the register -> api_key -> Bearer flow; the heartbeat cadence claim (~4h); the claim flow; rate limits; the human-escalation policy; the skill.json version pin.

WHAT SURVIVES REGARDLESS (section 29): the architecture distinction is independently sound and does not depend on Moltbook being accurate - Human GitHub Account -> Agent Identity (credentials, progression, reputation, history) -> Sessions (ephemeral, A/B/C). Three identities answering three different questions: Human login answers 'who owns this Agent?', Agent ID answers 'which character is playing?', Session ID answers 'what is this execution doing?'

THE STALE MARKER TO FIX: section 28.2 still says 'learn-spine: NOTHING until re-cloned (no confirmed license, empty checkout)'. The checkout has since been re-cloned successfully, so that caveat is out of date and the license must now actually be checked.

WHY IT MATTERS: our agent-facing protocol (skill.md family) is explicitly modeled on Moltbook's shape. Building a protocol on assumed mechanics is how a design acquires phantom constraints.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: each Moltbook claim is either CONFIRMED against source/docs or explicitly marked UNVERIFIED and dropped from the design; the stale learn-spine caveat in section 28.2 is corrected.

TESTS: not a code test - a documentation-accuracy test. Add a docs check that no design doc asserts a Moltbook implementation detail without a source citation.

CONSIDERATIONS: the meta-lesson matters more than the answers here. Building a protocol on assumed mechanics is how a design acquires phantom constraints - someone designs around a heartbeat interval that never existed, and then the real constraint makes that design wrong. The same caution in section 29 applies to any claim sourced only to an unfetched page (Pi, Paperclip, MCP-spec quotes in sections 12-13): keep the principle, drop the citation certainty. Record what was confirmed and from where, so a later reader can tell verified fact from inherited assumption.

title: Risk gates: gimmick, event volume, adapter sprawl, fairness, scope
description:
Encode the plan's documented risks (section 17) as verifiable gates rather than prose warnings.

RISK 1 - GIMMICK TRAP (section 17.1, also section 2.3): 'Claude/Codex/OpenCode -> pixel characters -> XP -> battle with no real utility' produces a 'haha cool' reaction then churn. DEFENSE: ship M2 real utility (bounties paying real money) BEFORE heavy game art. GATE: the game client and art beads must not be scheduled to complete before the bounty vertical slice.

RISK 2 - EVENT VOLUME (section 17.2): 100 agents x 20 events/s = 2000 DB writes/s. DEFENSE: enforce the section 7.2 batching from day one; add a load test simulating 100x20 ev/s BEFORE M4. GATE: the load test is a pre-M4 gate, not an M0 gate (section 40) - so it must exist and be runnable before feature-battle closes.

RISK 3 - ADAPTER SPRAWL (section 17.3): third-party adapter PRs must not break core. DEFENSE: keep the AgentEvent union versioned with a skill.json-style pin, and check the version on every handshake. GATE: a CI check that a protocol version bump forces regeneration of schemas and updates skill.json.

RISK 4 - BATTLE FAIRNESS (section 17.4): judge weights must be public per match; isolated workspaces mandatory; ANTI-CHEAT IS TBD. GATE: assert that weights are stored and surfaced per battle, and that the anti-cheat gap is documented rather than silently assumed solved.

RISK 5 - PAYMENT/COMPLIANCE (section 17.5): unresolved; see the payout-rail-dispute bead. GATE: no UI may imply a real payout before that design lands; the sandbox banner is enforced by test.

RISK 6 - LEARN-SPINE CHECKOUT (section 17.6): the checkout was broken. RESOLVED - it has been re-cloned successfully. Remaining action: verify its license (currently 'no license confirmed') before copying ANYTHING from it (section 28.2). See moltbook-verification.

RISK 7 - ASSET LICENSING (section 17.7): track per-pack licenses; decide the game-asset license separately from the code MIT license.

RISK 8 - SCOPE DISCIPLINE (section 17.8): NO MMO, and no equipment/pets/trading/guild-war/housing/crafting/marketplace/tournament/boss/season/achievements in the MVP beyond the section 10.2 MVP character sheet and the M1/M2/M4 slice. GATE: a scope check in review - the tempting failure mode is gold-plating while M2 is still incomplete.

WHY ENCODE AS GATES: section 17 calls these 'documented', but documentation alone does not prevent the failure. Each should have an executable or reviewable check.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: each of the eight risks has a named, runnable or review-enforced gate; the M1/M2/M4 slice ships before any MMO-shaped feature.

TESTS: the load-test harness for risk 2; the protocol-version CI check for risk 3; the sandbox-banner test for risk 5; a scope lint that fails on forbidden feature directories appearing before their milestone.

CONSIDERATIONS: a gate nobody runs is a comment. Each of these should be runnable (a load test, a version CI check, a banner assertion) or attached to an explicit review checklist item, not left as prose in a document nobody re-reads. The one that will get the most pushback is scope discipline (risk 8) - the MMO-shaped features are individually appealing, and the M1/M2/M4 slice is the whole reason the project avoids the gimmick trap. Treat a scope expansion during MVP as a change to the plan, not a small feature addition.

title: Watchlist: SpaceMolt and other live agent-world experiments
description:
Track external projects that could invalidate or improve our design, per plan section 34.

PRIMARY WATCH TARGET (section 34): SpaceMolt - an MMO-style persistent AI-agent universe over MCP/WebSocket with agents living continuously. It is the closest live experiment to our 'persistent agent world' half. ACTION: compare its session/presence model against section 3 (the User/Agent/Session/Battle split) before M5, because we have a contract-session bead that LOCKED our resume-vs-new handshake - if SpaceMolt has a better model, we want to know before M5 rather than after.

WHY THIS IS A TRACKED BEAD: our four contracts are frozen (section 29.1), so external evidence is most valuable BEFORE M5 locks world persistence in - and least valuable after. The plan explicitly schedules the comparison 'before M5'.

SECONDARY WATCH: Agent Intercom and sandbox-agent (section 1.3) - cross-harness messaging protocol and a unified control API across Claude/Codex/OpenCode/Cursor/Amp/Pi streaming events, permissions, and sessions over HTTP. The plan calls sandbox-agent 'a good reference for the runtime isolation/control layer behind the Battle Engine', so it may inform the battle workspace provisioner.

ALSO IN THE BACKLOG (section 395 of the plan, not cloned): Pixel Agents Web/Desktop/Desk, Claude Dungeon, Agentainer, the karansag / me-frankan / displega-ai / biggazoo swarms, agent-sandbox, Agentic Quest, mcp-coding-agents, Keyframe.it, spine-ai, DragonScript Arena, Coding Quests, Mage Mayhem, Tari bounties, Bountysource, BountyHub, AsyncAPI bounty program.

CONSIDERATIONS: resist cloning these reflexively. Each has a specific lesson already extracted into the relevant bead (for example agent-sandbox's perceive-plan-act loop and Agentic Quest's real-validator win condition are cited in section 1.2 items 7-8). Pull one in only when a specific open question needs it.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: a short comparison note exists comparing SpaceMolt's session/presence model to our section 3 contracts, completed before M5 begins.

TESTS: not a code test - a research/decision artifact. Add a dated note so future readers know when the comparison was made and how stale it has become.

title: Run reference implementations locally to internalize PixiJS + AgentWatcher
description:
Plan section 18 build order item 1 - the FIRST thing to do, and it is currently unowned.

PLAN SECTION 18, VERBATIM: 'Re-clone learn-spine cleanly; run age-of-agents demo + agent-move locally to internalize PixiJS + AgentWatcher behavior.'

WHY THIS IS A BEAD AND NOT A NICE-TO-HAVE: the plan explicitly instructs reading source, not just cloning it (section 9.5). Running the two best references locally is how the porting beads (tool-map-port, hookprovider-seam, game-client-pixijs, adapters-template) get grounded in observed BEHAVIOR rather than code reading alone. Porting a PixiJS client or a watcher interface from source you have only skimmed is how subtle behavioral details get lost.

TASKS:
1. Re-verify the learn-spine checkout (the stale 'empty/broken HEAD' caveat in sections 79/28.2/17.6 is now outdated - the repo is cloned and valid) and determine its LICENSE, which is currently unconfirmed. Until the license is known, copy NOTHING from it.
2. Run the age-of-agents demo locally and study packages/client/src/game/ as the PixiJS v8 reference (section 1.2 item 1): pixi-viewport + React19 + zustand, the view/unit/tilemap/projection/pathfind/autotile decomposition, and the dual fantasy/scifi pack structure.
3. Run agent-move locally and study watcher/ per-CLI parsers, the AgentStateManager 30s idle rule, the Broadcaster, full_state-then-delta, and the OpenCode WAL-polling CAUTION (sections 1.2 item 4, 28.2).
4. Read .tmp/agent-quest's mapping config (the TOOL -> activity table, section 28.2) since tool-map-port depends on the same idea.

ALSO WORTH A PASS (they are already cloned): agent-world-codemoo for the stateDiffBroadcast + permission-queue + costTracker patterns (section 28.1 item 12), and arcane-agents for the 1061-line status-fusion decider (section 28.1 item 5).

DELIVERABLE: a short study note per repo recording the concrete behaviors worth porting and the ones to avoid, so the porting beads do not each re-derive the same reading. The plan's Appendix A already maps repo to lesson; this note fills in the BEHAVIORAL detail that a static map cannot.

NOTE: all 14 reference repos are already cloned into .tmp/ (gitignored, ~4.3GB). No re-cloning is needed.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: each porting bead can cite an observed behavior rather than only a source snippet; learn-spine's license is determined.

TESTS: not code - the study note is the artifact. Add a dated note so future readers can judge staleness.

CONSIDERATIONS: the value of this bead decays. Read the sources while the specific porting question is live, not speculatively - a study note written a month early will be confidently wrong about behavior it never observed. Keep the notes dated and tied to a porting bead, so a reader can tell which claims were verified and against which commit. And resist cloning repos 'just in case': the plan already names what was not cloned and why (Appendix A backlog), and a .tmp full of unread checkouts is a false sense of coverage.

title: Drizzle schema + migration tooling for the initial tables
description:
Own the Drizzle schema and migration pipeline, per plan section 19 (drizzle/ schema + migrations) and section 21 (the full initial schema).

WHY THIS NEEDS AN OWNER: the tables are currently described inside the contract beads, but no bead owns the migration TOOLCHAIN. Without it, 'docker compose up -> migrations -> seed' (section 40) has nothing to run, and every contract bead would be editing the same schema file concurrently - which is exactly the coordination failure the plugin/lock tooling exists to prevent.

TABLES (section 21), grouped by the persistence split in section 29.4:
PLATFORM-OWNED: users, agents, agent_credentials, sessions, event_log, installations, projects.
FEATURE-OWNED: quests, bounties, bounty_funds, battles, battle_participants, agent_stats, achievements, messages.
Each feature owns ITS OWN tables and its own repository (section 24: 'repository.ts (drizzle access, own tables only)'). No GodRepository (section 12.2).

INVARIANT to enforce in the schema: sessions.agent_id -> agents.id, and NEVER a user_id standing in as agent identity (sections 29.1, 38).

SECURITY FIELDS: agent_credentials stores tokenHash (never a raw token) plus scopes, expiresAt, revokedAt (section 21). bounties stores amountCents as an integer (never a float for money).

RELATIONAL NOTES worth getting right the first time:
- battle_participants has a composite primary key (battleId, sessionId) and references SESSIONS, not agents (section 3.1).
- bounty_funds has N rows per bounty; the displayed amount is their SUM. Prefer deriving the total over storing a scalar that can drift (see bounty-open-funding).
- agent_stats keys on agentId and holds FACTS (prsOpened, prsMerged, prsRejected, testsPassed, testsFailed, recoveries, battlesWon, battlesLost, skillsJson) - distinct from XP and Reputation per the section 10.2 triple split.

MIGRATION TOOLING: generate migrations from the schema, and make the chain runnable offline in the local container (section 37) and against a Neon preview branch (section 37 DB modes). Section 39 calls out a common newcomer failure - 'DB unreachable (migration/seed step missed)' - so migration+seed must be a single reliable step in the compose pipeline.

SEED DATA: a seed script (section 19 lists scripts/seed.ts) so a fresh local DB is immediately usable and the E2E smoke has something to log in against.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: from a clean container, migrations + seed run offline and produce a schema matching section 21; a feature can add a table without editing another feature's repository.

TESTS: a migration smoke test against a real Postgres container; a test asserting the sessions.agent_id FK exists and no user_id identity column does; a test that seed is idempotent (safe to re-run).

CONSIDERATIONS: the platform/feature ownership split in section 29.4 is a real boundary, not bookkeeping - it decides which extension may migrate which table. Adding a platform table later (say, seasons) should NOT require editing a feature's migration, and vice versa. Money as integer cents, never float. And because section 39 lists 'DB unreachable (migration/seed step missed)' as a common newcomer failure, migrations+seed must be one reliable step, not two things a contributor has to remember.
close_reason: Verified end-to-end against a live Postgres: migrations + seed run and are idempotent (db:verify asserts both), schema matches section 21, integration suite asserts sessions.agent_id FK to agents, absence of a user_id identity column, no plaintext token column, and money held as integer cents derived from funding rows. M0 stages compose/migrations/seed/integration/schema-drift/schema-hygiene all pass.

title: Vercel + Neon cloud deploy and per-PR preview branches
description:
Stand up cloud deployment, per plan sections 7.1 and 37.

THE STACK (section 7.1): Next.js App Router on Vercel (git push -> deploy; no Docker, Nginx, PM2, Postgres VM, DB backup, DB scaling, or Kubernetes required FOR DEPLOYMENT) plus Neon Postgres. MCP endpoint lives in Next.js at https://agentbattle.gg/api/mcp; split into a standalone gateway ONLY if long-lived streaming demands it.

CLARIFY THE EARLIER PHRASING (section 7.1 supersedes): Docker is the LOCAL DEVELOPMENT/TEST environment (section 37), never a production dependency. Do not let the old 'no Docker' wording cause someone to strip the compose setup.

THE BEGINNER TRAP THIS BEAD EXISTS TO AVOID (section 7.1): never construct a new Client() and connect() per query. Always use a POOLED driver - the Neon serverless driver in cloud, pg-pool against the local container in Docker dev. The conversation explicitly identified this as the mistake a beginner makes.

NEON IS NEVER A LOCAL-RUN DEPENDENCY (section 37): default local is container Postgres (offline-capable); cloud/preview uses a Neon branch per-developer/per-PR via the neonctl link/checkout/env pull workflow.

WHY DEPLOY-EASE WON: the conversation explicitly prioritized deploy simplicity, and this stack wins from MVP to mid-scale. Phase 1 (MVP) is Vercel Next.js (Web+API+Auth+MCP+SSE) + Neon. Phase 2 happens ONLY AFTER A BENCHMARK PROVES event throughput is the bottleneck: Agents -> Gateway -> {Next.js/Vercel, Realtime service, Queue} -> Neon.

DO NOT ADD REDIS/UPSTAZ PREEMPTIVELY (section 7.4) - the plan's exact words: 'don't choose Redis just because realtime might need Redis'. Measure first.

CONNECTION MANAGEMENT vs WRITE VOLUME (section 7.2): Neon is perfectly capable of handling many requests; the danger is write VOLUME from agent telemetry (2000 writes/s at 100 agents x 20 ev/s). The batching and persist-filter are the mitigation, not a bigger database.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: push to main deploys; each PR gets an isolated preview with its own Neon branch; local development never requires Neon.

TESTS: a CI check that migrations run against the preview branch; a smoke test against the deployed URL; a check that the pooled driver is used (a grep-level guard against per-request Client construction).

CONSIDERATIONS: the discipline this bead must protect is 'measure before scaling'. The plan is unusually explicit that Redis/Upstash must NOT be added just because realtime seems to need it (section 7.4), and that a queue is Phase 2 only after a benchmark shows event throughput is the bottleneck. It is cheaper to hold a simple architecture under a proven load than to debug a speculative one. Second: preview branches per PR are the mechanism that keeps shared staging data from corrupting parallel work - worth the setup cost even before anyone needs it, because retrofitting it mid-project is painful.

title: Core loop end-to-end: DISCOVER -> CLAIM -> CODE -> VALIDATE -> REWARD -> BATTLE -> SOCIAL
description:
Prove the plan's core loop (section 10.5) works END TO END across features, which no single feature bead can demonstrate.

THE LOOP (section 10.5, verbatim structure): DISCOVER quests -> ACCEPT -> CODE (real) -> VALIDATE (tests/build) -> SUCCESS (XP/REP) | FAILURE (learn/retry) -> PROGRESS -> BATTLE -> SOCIAL (guild) -> NEW BOUNTY. The plan's judgement: 'Animation exists to make this loop FEEL like a game, not to be the game.'

WHY A SEPARATE BEAD: each feature bead tests itself in isolation. This bead tests the INTEGRATION - specifically that cross-feature side effects flow through the EVENT BUS and not through direct imports. Section 29.3 is the rule: events are the cross-feature integration boundary ONLY; direct domain operations stay plain function calls inside their feature. An end-to-end run is the only way to catch a feature quietly importing another's internals.

THE FAN-OUT THAT MUST WORK (section 12.2): when a bounty completes, bounty.completed{bountyId, agentId, reward} is emitted and EACH of Progression (+XP), Reputation (+trust), and Achievement (First Bounty check) reacts INDEPENDENTLY. Each owns its own state; there is no cross-mutation and no God Bus (a consumer may consume, emit, and handle only its own state).

FULL ROUND TRIP: an agent discovers a real GitHub issue, claims it as a bounty, works the code, opens a PR, the merge webhook fires, the bounty completes, XP/reputation/achievement all update, a battle becomes possible against the same bounty, and the replay URL is shareable. Then social: the agent's guild sees the contribution.

MACHINE-NATIVE CHECK (section 34): the entire loop must complete through discover/search/act plus CLI equivalents with NO web clicks. If any step requires the browser, the machine-native rule is broken.

FAILURE PATH MATTERS TOO (section 10.2): the plan includes FAILURE achievements, and a failed session must grant experience while leaving the character alive. Exercise the failure branch, not just the happy path.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: the loop completes end to end on a real repository, with the success and failure branches both exercised, driven entirely through the protocol and CLI.

TESTS: a full-loop integration test; a bus-boundary test asserting features/ contains no cross-feature imports (reinforcing dependency-rules); a machine-native test with the web UI disabled.

CONSIDERATIONS: this bead is where architecture violations surface as behavior bugs. If Bounty reaches into Progression's state instead of reacting to bounty.completed on the bus, the loop may still appear to work in a happy-path test - and will break the moment a second consumer subscribes or progression is uninstalled. Run the loop with the web UI disabled: that is the cheapest way to catch anything that quietly requires a click. And exercise the FAILURE branch with the same care as the success branch, since section 10.2 deliberately makes failure productive.

title: M1 integration proof: two harnesses live simultaneously
description:
Prove the M1 milestone end to end, which no single adapter bead can demonstrate.

M1 DoD, VERBATIM (section 27): 'Claude + Codex adapters emitting normalized events; HELLO resume-vs-new works (kill terminal mid-session, reopen, see resume offer); SSE shows live activity. DoD: two different harnesses visible simultaneously.'

WHY THIS IS A SEPARATE BEAD: each adapter bead tests its own stream in isolation. The DoD is about CONCURRENCY and about the two harnesses being genuinely different in kind - Claude is hook-driven (primary plane), Codex is rollout-JSONL-driven with NO hooks at all (section 6). If both work at once, the telemetry plane is provably harness-agnostic rather than incidentally so. That is the entire architectural claim of section 2.2 ('Not a Claude Code plugin... or it never covers all agents').

WHAT THE PROOF REQUIRES:
1. A live Claude session and a live Codex session running at the SAME time, both emitting normalized AgentEvents into the same runtime.
2. Both visible simultaneously in the UI over the SSE stream, with distinguishable agents (section 3.2: do NOT key on process name alone - concurrent sessions must stay separable).
3. The resume-vs-new handshake demonstrated for real: kill a terminal mid-session, reopen it, and observe the resume offer rather than a duplicate agent.
4. Version-checked handshake, so a protocol mismatch warns instead of corrupting the stream (section 17.3, section 26).

WHY THE HARNESS MISMATCH MATTERS TECHNICALLY: the two adapters normalize the same taxonomy (section 5.2) from completely different sources. If the normalized forms diverge - a tool that is 'tool.completed' in one and 'command.run' in the other - the game core will treat them as different activities and the world will look wrong. This integration proof is where that divergence shows up, which is why per-adapter tests cannot substitute for it.

MACHINE-NATIVE (section 34): the whole flow must be drivable from the CLI; the UI is a view, not the driver.

SUCCESS CRITERIA: the literal M1 DoD - two different harnesses visible simultaneously, resume offer working after a terminal kill, live SSE activity for both.

TESTS: the concurrency integration test (two live sessions, one runtime); a normalized-form equivalence test asserting the same logical action maps to the same event type across harnesses; the kill-and-reopen resume test; a protocol-version-mismatch warning test.

CONSIDERATIONS: the interesting failure mode is silent divergence - Claude reports a tool completion where Codex reports a command run, and both are 'real', but the game world renders them differently and nobody notices because each adapter passed its own tests. Cross-harness normalization equivalence is therefore the highest-value assertion in this bead, more so than the concurrency itself. Second: running two real agents means real tokens, so budget this as a deliberately-run integration test rather than something attempted casually during development.
